item.title: Four months after Rafael: what the crude market learned about depending on one channel
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Exports are back and the anchorage is busy. An analyst says the lesson of the fall was not the storm but the share: about half of U.S. crude exports through a single entrance.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Four months after Hurricane Rafael, crude is loading at Corpus Christi at a pace close to what it was before the storm. Reviews of port security are among several still under way.

Sabal asked Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics who has tracked the port's flows through both closures, what the market took from the fall.

"We always knew the share was large," Holloway said. "We learned what it feels like when the share is zero."

The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports. It was closed for a month from mid-September, partly reopened with spill restrictions for two more weeks, and then closed for 14 days in November.

Holloway drew three lessons.

The system has more cushion than expected, and less than people now assume. Storage absorbed a month of halted exports. "It worked once from a standing start. The second time the tanks were already part full. I would not count on a third," she said.

Closures are not all the same kind. The first was weather and a spill. The second was a security event. "The market knows how to wait for a survey. It did not know how to wait for an all-clear. Now it has done both."

Alternatives are now written down. Buyers have second ports in their contracts, and forwarders of other cargo have done the same. "That is a permanent change. It costs a little every day and saves a great deal on the bad day," she said.

What has not changed is the geography. One entrance at Port Aransas still serves the whole port.

Federal agencies issued a maritime cyber advisory in late December on vendor access to tanker cargo systems, and investigations from the fall have not all reported.

"Hurricane season is the date everyone circles," Holloway said. "This year people will also be reading the security reviews. That is new."

Loadings continue normally.

item.title: Federal filing: Navy's suspended fuel supplier and storm debris hauler share an offshore owner
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: A civil forfeiture filing says Quellmar Fuel Partners and Vantorra Restoration are owned by Brannoch Maritime Holdings and that accounts tied to them received about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Quellmar Fuel Partners, the emergency fuel supplier suspended by the Navy, and Vantorra Restoration, a storm debris hauler, share an owner, an offshore company called Brannoch Maritime Holdings, according to a federal civil forfeiture filing made public Thursday.

The filing lists Brannoch's director as L. Marrick. It says bank accounts tied to the two firms received about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid. It does not say how the aid was diverted.

A civil forfeiture case is brought against money or property, not against a person. Its claims are allegations that have not been proven in court, and no one has been criminally charged.

"All product Quellmar delivered met specifications," Nadia Kerr, the company's operations manager, said in a statement. "The company will respond in court."

Vantorra said it would respond through its attorneys.

Quellmar holds a $2.1 million emergency contract to supply fuel to Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. The Navy suspended it in November pending a fuel quality review. FBI agents searched the offices of both companies on Dec. 27.

For the fuel trade, the filing shifts attention from product quality to ownership. Emergency fuel contracts are awarded on a supplier's ability to deliver within days. Who stands behind the supplier is seldom examined at that speed.

A compliance adviser to fuel distributors, who asked not to be named, said he expected government buyers to tighten disclosure rules. "Ownership questions are normal in a competitive bid. In an emergency award they get skipped," he said. "I would expect that to change, and I would expect suppliers with complicated ownership to be asked to simplify it or sit out."

The filing does not allege that the fuel supplied to the air station was defective. The Navy has not released the results of its fuel quality review.

A federal inspector general's review of emergency fuel and debris contracts in the Coastal Bend, opened in December, is continuing.

item.title: Attribution puts Gulf export security on traders' radar
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: U.S. officials blamed a foreign government for the channel devices that halted Corpus Christi crude exports for 14 days. Analysts say security now sits beside weather in shipping risk.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — U.S. officials' attribution of the Corpus Christi ship channel devices and a tanker cyber intrusion to a foreign government adds a new line to the risk ledger for the largest U.S. crude export gateway, analysts said Wednesday.

The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports. Exports halted after an Oct. 28 explosion near the Port Aransas jetties, which the Navy said was caused by an explosive device, and resumed when the channel reopened Nov. 11 after 14 days.

"Until yesterday, the market could file the blast as a one-off with no name on it. Now it has a category: a government trying to exploit a hurricane," said Grace Holloway of Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "That doesn't move a barrel today. It moves how buyers and insurers think about the next storm."

Holloway said the questions from buyers will change. "It used to be, how fast does the channel reopen after a hurricane. Now it's also, who's watching the channel while everyone's watching the storm," she said.

The channel's two closures this fall came for different reasons, Holloway noted: Hurricane Rafael in September, the blast in October. "One of those you could see coming on a forecast map. The other one, officials are now telling us, was somebody trying to take advantage of the first," she said.

Officials called the intrusion and the devices attempts to exploit Hurricane Rafael but did not name the government. That came a week after the Coast Guard and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency told vessel operators to review the remote access their vendors have to cargo systems.

Holloway said she expects tanker operators and charterers to ask more questions about vendor access and channel security before booking Gulf Coast cargoes for the summer. "None of it changes the barrels. It changes the paperwork," she said.

The channel remains open.

item.title: Corpus Christi plans to harden power feeds to water plant that failed in Rafael
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The O.N. Stevens plant lost both of its feeds early in the storm, setting off five weeks of boil-water notices. The city says the fix starts with the electricity.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The City of Corpus Christi plans to harden the power feeds to the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, the facility whose failure during Hurricane Rafael left the city under boil-water notices for five weeks, the city water utility said.

The plant lost both of its power feeds early in the storm. Its pumps were damaged, pressure fell across the system and the utility ran on temporary pumps until replacement parts arrived in October.

"The pumps were damaged because the power failed first," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokeswoman for the city water utility. "We are starting where the failure started."

Gallegos did not give a cost or a schedule. She said details would go to the city council.

For utilities and the industries that depend on them, the plan addresses a weakness that Rafael exposed plainly. A treatment plant with two power feeds is designed so that one can fail. At O.N. Stevens, both did.

Hardening can take several forms, engineers say: strengthening or burying lines, routing the two feeds so that a single event cannot take out both, and adding on-site generation large enough to run the main pumps. Each costs more than the last.

The announcement comes as the state reviews separate storm procedures, including when bridges close in high winds.

Energy companies along the ship channel will watch the outcome. Terminals and refineries have their own arrangements for water and power, but their workers and the city's services do not. During the recovery, analysts repeatedly pointed to utilities as a limit on how fast the port could restart once the channel opened.

A plant operations consultant, who asked not to be named because she has worked for the city, said the lesson reaches beyond water. "Everybody had two feeds on paper. The storm asked whether they were really two," she said.

The utility's separate review of its control-system security, begun after a federal investigation into unauthorized access, is continuing.

item.title: Maritime cyber advisory hands charterers a new vetting question for tankers
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The Coast Guard and CISA want vessel operators to review who can reach cargo systems remotely. Buyers lifting crude are deciding whether to ask for proof.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — A joint advisory from the Coast Guard and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency urging vessel operators to review vendor remote access to cargo systems is prompting crude buyers to consider adding the question to how they vet tankers.

The advisory was issued Tuesday. It follows more than three months of investigation into possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of two tankers at Corpus Christi, from which an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released as Hurricane Rafael arrived.

"We are asking operators to know who holds a key to the cargo system and to be able to take it back," said Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with CISA. "Review vendor access. Keep cargo control separate from other networks. Log every session."

Tran declined to discuss the investigation.

The advisory does not impose new rules. Its commercial effect may come through charterers, who decide which ships they are willing to hire.

"An advisory is voluntary. A charterer's questionnaire is not," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "If the big buyers start asking for evidence of an access review before they fix a ship, every owner will have one within a month."

Holloway said she knew of no buyer that had formally changed its vetting requirements. She said several were discussing it. Terminals are having a parallel conversation, she said, about what they should know regarding a ship's systems before it connects to a loading arm.

The vendor at the center of the Corpus Christi case, Brightwake Marine Systems, said in September that its remote-maintenance access had been misused and that it had shut off all remote connections to customer vessels.

Holloway said the cost of compliance is small against the cost of a spill. "This is paperwork and a few difficult phone calls. Owners will do it. The question is whether they do it before the next charterer asks or after."

The Coast Guard has not released findings from its investigation.

item.title: FBI searches offices of Navy's suspended fuel supplier and a storm debris hauler
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Agents executed warrants at Quellmar Fuel Partners and Vantorra Restoration. Neither company has been charged. Quellmar says its fuel met specifications.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — FBI agents executed search warrants Monday at the offices of Quellmar Fuel Partners, the emergency fuel supplier suspended by the Navy last month, and Vantorra Restoration, a debris hauler hired by Nueces County after Hurricane Rafael.

"I can confirm that agents executed search warrants at both locations today," said Mark Ellery, a spokesman for the FBI's Houston Division. "I will not comment on what was sought or on the investigation."

Neither company has been charged with a crime. A search warrant requires a judge's approval and allows agents to look for evidence. It is not an accusation.

Quellmar holds a $2.1 million emergency contract to supply fuel to Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, awarded after the station's regular supplier flooded. The Navy suspended the company in late November pending a fuel quality review linked to a failure of the station's backup generator.

In a written statement, Quellmar said its product met specifications and that it is cooperating with authorities. Operations manager Nadia Kerr did not respond to a request for an interview.

Emergency debris and fuel contracts in the Coastal Bend have been under review by a federal inspector general since early December. Officials have not said whether the searches are connected to that review.

For the fuel trade, the searches raise the stakes of what began as a quality dispute. A suspension pending tests is a commercial matter. Search warrants are not.

A fuel distributor in South Texas, who asked not to be named, said customers had begun asking his company for documents they had not requested before. "They want the paper trail back to the rack," he said, using the industry term for the terminal where trucks load. "After this, I expect every emergency contract to ask for it up front."

The Navy has not released results of its fuel quality review.

Sabal will update this report if the companies respond further.

item.title: Corpus Christi ends the year loading normally; buyers keep the backup plans they wrote this fall
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The channel has been open six weeks and the anchorage is back to routine waits. What has not returned, an analyst says, is the assumption that the port is always there.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude is loading normally at Corpus Christi in the last full week of the year, six weeks after the ship channel reopened from the second of two closures this fall.

Tankers are again waiting at the offshore anchorage, which before September was a sign of a busy port and is being read that way again.

"The volume came back. The assumption did not," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Every buyer I talk to has a second port written down now."

The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports. It was shut for a month after Hurricane Rafael, with spill restrictions lasting two weeks longer, and for 14 days in November after explosive devices were found at the entrance.

Holloway said the lasting effect is in contracts, not flows. Buyers are asking for the right to load elsewhere if Corpus Christi closes, and for clearer terms on who pays when a ship waits. "Those clauses existed. People used to skip the page," she said.

She said sellers have largely agreed, because the alternative is losing the buyer. "Flexibility has a cost, and for now the seller is carrying some of it."

The port said it understands the caution. "We are closing the year with our customers shipping," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "We will spend next year earning the word reliable back."

Three matters from the fall remain unresolved and could bear on that. The Coast Guard has not released findings on possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo systems of two tankers involved in the September spill. The FBI is still investigating the devices at the entrance. And no agency has explained a spoofed vessel identity seen near the channel in October.

"None of those stops a cargo today," Holloway said. "All of them are why the second port is written down."

Loadings are expected to continue through the holidays.

item.title: Corpus Christi spill claims move to lost income as tanker owners' tab stays open
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: A claims center run for the owners of the two tankers that spilled crude during Hurricane Rafael has added lost-income claims to cleanup and property claims. No total has been released.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Three months after about 9,000 barrels of crude spilled from two tankers at an Inner Harbor terminal in Corpus Christi, the cost of the release is still being counted through a claims center run for the vessels' owners, which has widened from cleanup and property claims to lost income.

The center opened Sept. 26 for spill cleanup and property damage claims and began taking lost-income claims from fishers and shoreline businesses Nov. 16, as federal oil spill law requires. If the owners' center has not paid a claim within 90 days, the claimant can turn to the Coast Guard's National Pollution Funds Center.

The two tankers, MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, were moored at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived in mid-September. Surge and wind spread sheen across about 33 square miles of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. Fishing there remains closed by Texas Parks and Wildlife and shellfish harvesting by the Texas Department of State Health Services.

"The claims center is the owners' obligation, not the state's. Our job is making sure people know it exists and actually file," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "For a shrimper, that means trip logs and fuel receipts. For a shoreline business, it means the books."

Victor Lang, a spokesman for Rendal Terminals, which operates the berth, said claims tied to the vessels go through the owners' claims center. "Our position hasn't changed. Rendal is cooperating fully, and questions about the vessels belong with their owners," he said.

How the release happened is still unresolved. In September the Coast Guard said it was looking at whether someone gained unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems, and Brightwake Marine Systems, a vendor for those systems, said its remote-maintenance credentials were misused and cut off all remote access. Investigators have released no findings.

Neither the claims center nor the Unified Command has released a count or dollar total of claims filed so far.

item.title: Corpus Christi crude heads into year-end after two fall shutdowns
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Exports from the largest U.S. crude gateway resumed when the ship channel reopened Nov. 11. The bigger question for next year is confidence, not capacity, an analyst says.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from Corpus Christi head into the final weeks of the year with the ship channel open, after a fall in which shipments halted twice: first when the Coast Guard closed the port to inbound traffic Sept. 12 ahead of Hurricane Rafael, and again after an Oct. 28 explosion at the Port Aransas jetties shut it for 14 days.

The port handles an outsized share of U.S. crude exports, about half by analysts' estimates. Before the storm it was loading tankers at near-record pace, and exports hit a monthly high at the end of August.

"Two closures in one quarter, from two completely different causes. That's what buyers will remember," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Exports resumed when the channel reopened. The question now is confidence, not capacity."

The first shutdown outlasted the storm. The channel partly reopened Oct. 14, but spill decontamination kept the inner channel restricted until Oct. 28, and an anchorage backlog delayed cargoes; 14 vessels had queued offshore when the port closed to inbound traffic. The second halt came Oct. 28, the same day the inner-channel restrictions were lifted, when a blast beside a harbor tug closed the channel again. Navy teams found and rendered safe a second device Nov. 5, and the channel reopened Nov. 11 after a full sweep.

"The channel is open, and we're moving barrels," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi.

Holloway said the open investigation keeps some uncertainty in the market. The FBI is investigating the blast, and officials have not said who was responsible.

"Markets can price a hurricane. There's a century of data on hurricanes," she said. "An open question is harder to price."

item.title: Federal inspector general to review emergency fuel and debris contracts awarded after Rafael
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The review covers contracts across the Coastal Bend, including the fuel deal now suspended by the Navy. Suppliers say they will cooperate.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — A federal inspector general has opened a review of emergency debris and fuel contracts awarded in the Coastal Bend after Hurricane Rafael.

The review was announced Tuesday. It did not name individual contracts.

Two have drawn public attention. Quellmar Fuel Partners holds a $2.1 million emergency contract to supply fuel to Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. The Navy suspended the company late last month pending a fuel quality review linked to a backup generator failure at the station. The company says its fuel meets specifications.

Separately, records show that Vantorra Restoration, which holds a county debris contract, billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own surveys estimated. The company denies overbilling. The county has paused payments pending an audit.

"Quellmar will cooperate with the inspector general, as we are cooperating with the Navy," said Nadia Kerr, the company's operations manager. "We stand by our product."

Inspector general reviews of disaster contracts are common after large storms. They examine whether awards made under emergency rules followed the law, whether prices were reasonable and whether the government received what it paid for.

For energy suppliers, the fuel side of the review is the relevant part. Emergency fuel contracts are typically awarded within days, to whichever supplier can deliver, and often without competitive bids. Reviewers generally look at how a supplier was chosen, where its product came from and whether delivery records match invoices.

A review is not an accusation, and none of the companies has been charged with wrongdoing.

Suppliers that delivered fuel under emergency contracts in the region after the storm should expect requests for records, a procurement lawyer who asked not to be named told Sabal. "Keep everything. Bills of lading, test certificates, tank gauges. If you have it, the review is short," she said.

The inspector general's office gave no timetable.

item.title: Navy suspends emergency fuel supplier to Corpus Christi air station pending quality review
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Quellmar Fuel Partners won a $2.1 million emergency contract after the storm. The review is linked to a backup generator failure at the station in October. The company says its fuel meets specifications.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The Navy has suspended Quellmar Fuel Partners, the emergency fuel supplier to Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, pending a fuel quality review linked to a backup generator failure at the station, the Navy said Sunday.

Quellmar was awarded a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for the air station after the station's regular supplier flooded in Hurricane Rafael, federal contract records show.

The station's backup generator failed during a power interruption in late October. Power was restored and the cause was placed under review.

"The station has suspended deliveries from its emergency fuel supplier pending a fuel quality review," said Lt. Marcus Hale, public affairs officer for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. "There is no impact to operations."

Hale did not say what the review had found so far or how long it would take.

Quellmar disputed any suggestion that its product was at fault. "All product Quellmar delivered met specifications," said Nadia Kerr, the company's operations manager. "We are cooperating with the Navy's review and we expect it to confirm that."

A suspension is not a finding. It stops deliveries while the Navy tests fuel and examines records.

For fuel buyers, the case is a reminder of how emergency procurement works after a disaster. When a regular supplier is knocked out, agencies can award contracts quickly and without the usual competition. Speed is the purpose. It also means less time to check a new supplier's sources and handling.

Fuel quality reviews typically look at samples retained from each delivery, the paperwork that traces product back to a refinery or terminal, and the condition of the tanks it passed through. Water and sediment are the most common problems in stored diesel, and either can stop a generator.

The Navy has not said where it is obtaining fuel for the station's backup systems in the meantime.

Kerr said Quellmar would respond to any questions from the Navy. She declined to discuss the company's supply sources.

item.title: Corpus Christi crude flows recover after reopening as catch-up continues
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Eleven days after the ship channel reopened, loadings are back and the offshore queue has eased. An analyst says the lasting effect may be in how buyers price the port.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi have largely recovered in the 11 days since the ship channel reopened after a 14-day closure, with tankers that waited offshore working through the berths and onshore storage drawing down, market participants said Monday.

The port is the outlet for about half of U.S. crude exports, according to analysts. Exports were halted from the Oct. 28 explosion near the Port Aransas jetties until the Coast Guard reopened the channel Nov. 11 after a full sweep by Navy teams.

"The physical side is catching up about as you'd expect: the queue first, then the tanks," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "What takes longer is the paperwork side. Some cargoes were rebooked from other ports during the closure, and those contracts don't all swing back at once."

Holloway said the bigger question for the coming year is how buyers weigh this fall's back-to-back shutdowns. "Weather risk is priced every season. This fall added something buyers hadn't really priced at this port before," she said. "The sweep and the reopening went cleanly, and that helps. But people will be asking about it in every contract negotiation this winter."

The reopening also allowed a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment to load onto a sealift ship and sail for an overseas rotation, the Army said, after two delays.

The FBI is investigating the Oct. 28 explosion. Beyond the Navy's statement that an explosive device caused the blast, officials have said nothing about a cause.

Holloway said she expects export volumes to be close to normal by early December if no new disruptions occur. "That's a forecast, not a promise," she said. "This year taught everybody that."

item.title: Regulators close emergency phase of Corpus Christi spill response after 60-day assessment
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: State and federal agencies say hydrocarbon levels in Corpus Christi Bay are back below the state standard. Long-term monitoring and the owners' claims process continue.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — State and federal environmental regulators have closed the emergency response phase of the Corpus Christi oil spill after a 60-day assessment found hydrocarbon levels in Corpus Christi Bay back below the state surface water standard.

The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality and the Environmental Protection Agency's regional office released the assessment Saturday. They said shoreline cleanup in Nueces Bay is nearly complete, with a short stretch near the Nueces Bay Causeway to be addressed in a spring maintenance program. Water quality at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant has remained within regulatory limits for more than seven weeks.

Long-term ecological monitoring of seagrass and oyster habitat in Nueces Bay will continue under a separate natural resource damage assessment, the agencies said.

"The emergency is over. The monitoring is not, and neither is the claims process," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program, which formed the Unified Command with the Coast Guard after the spill.

An estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released from two tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived. The spill kept part of the ship channel under restrictions until late October.

For the energy sector, the assessment formally ends the spill as an operating constraint on the port. The practical end came earlier, when inner-channel restrictions were lifted.

What remains is cost. A claims center run for the tankers' owners has been taking cleanup and property damage claims since September. Fishing closures in the bays are still in place.

And cause. The Coast Guard has said investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems. No findings have been released, and the question of who ultimately bears the cost of the spill depends on them.

The ship channel reopened Thursday after a separate two-week closure. Crude loadings have resumed.

Whitaker said residents who find tar balls should report them and should not handle them.

item.title: First crude cargoes sail from Corpus Christi as channel works through its first full day open
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Loaded tankers held inside for two weeks are leaving, ships are coming in from the anchorage, and military sealift is sharing the schedule.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Loaded crude tankers held inside the port for two weeks sailed from Corpus Christi on Friday, the first full day of operations since the ship channel reopened.

The Coast Guard lifted its closure order Thursday after a 14-day closure and a full sweep of the channel by Navy and Coast Guard teams.

"Tankers out, tankers in, and the Army's cargo loading," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "That is a good day."

The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports. Ships that waited at the offshore anchorage are being brought in under a sequence agreed with the pilots.

The channel is also carrying military cargo. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment, delayed twice this fall, began loading onto a sealift ship and will sail over the next five days.

"This restart is cleaner than October's," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "One constraint, and it is gone."

When the channel partly reopened after Hurricane Rafael, spill decontamination restricted the inner channel for two more weeks and the backlog cleared slowly. Those restrictions ended before the latest closure. Holloway said that should let loadings recover faster this time.

She said the first days would be dominated by ships already loaded or already waiting. New fixtures for Corpus Christi cargoes would follow as buyers regained confidence. "The physical recovery is quick. The commercial one takes longer. People who booked other ports will finish those voyages," she said.

Storage along the channel, which filled during the closure, is beginning to draw down.

Holloway said she expected questions about security at the entrance to continue. The FBI investigation into the explosive devices found there remains open. "The channel is open. The file is not closed," she said.

The Coast Guard said port condition is normal.

item.title: Corpus Christi crude loadings resume after 14-day halt
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The reopening restores the largest U.S. crude export gateway. Analysts say the restart will be measured in days of catch-up, not hours.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from the Port of Corpus Christi resumed Thursday after the Coast Guard reopened the ship channel following a 14-day closure and a full sweep by Navy teams.

Roughly half of U.S. crude exports leave through the port, by analysts' count. Loadings had been halted since an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties Oct. 28, and a second explosive device found and rendered safe near the entrance Nov. 5 had extended the search.

"The door is open. Now comes the line," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Tankers that waited offshore come in first, storage onshore starts to drain, and the cargoes that were rebooked elsewhere don't all come back at once. Expect a catch-up period, not a snap back."

Holloway said traders would also watch for any lasting change in how buyers price risk at the port after two closures in two months, one from a hurricane and one from the blast. "Markets have short memories for weather and longer ones for security," she said. "The fact that the sweep was thorough helps. Buyers want to know the channel was cleared, not just opened."

The Coast Guard said traffic would resume under the direction of the Captain of the Port and pilots. The port said terminals were staffed and working around the clock.

The FBI is investigating the Oct. 28 explosion. Officials have not discussed a cause beyond the Navy's statement that it was caused by an explosive device.

item.title: Beyond crude: general cargo and relief freight stuck again behind Corpus Christi closure
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The forwarder whose relief containers waited a month offshore after Rafael says customers' cargo is held again. He is no longer planning around a single channel.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The closure of the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, now in its 14th day, is holding up more than crude.

Dry cargo, project freight and supplies bound for the hurricane recovery are waiting behind the same closed entrance as the tankers. For some shippers it is the second long delay in two months.

"I told my customers in October it would not happen twice," said Terry Akins, regional manager of Gulf Relief Logistics, a freight forwarder. "I have stopped saying that."

Akins's company booked 40 relief containers on the cargo ship MV Gulf Provider before Hurricane Rafael. The ship waited at the offshore anchorage through the storm closure and the backlog after the channel partly reopened, and berthed Oct. 17, about a month late.

He said customers' cargo is now held again. He would not say how much or for whom. "It is not forty boxes of water this time. It is the things people need to rebuild," he said.

The channel has been closed since an explosion near the Port Aransas jetties. Navy teams found and made safe a second explosive device last week and are still searching.

Akins said he does not question the closure. "Nobody wants a ship in there until the Navy says so. I want that more than anyone. My complaint is with my own plan," he said.

That plan is changing. Akins said he is moving some cargo by truck from other Gulf ports, at higher cost, and will write a second port into future contracts. "Corpus Christi is a good port. It has one door," he said.

Energy markets have focused on the crude export halt. The port handles a wide range of other cargo, and the same entrance serves all of it.

The Coast Guard has given no reopening date. Ships of all kinds continue to hold at the offshore anchorage.

Akins said he checks the Coast Guard's notices before he checks his email. "It is the only message that matters right now," he said.

item.title: Corpus Christi export halt hits 13th day; port says restart plan is written and waiting
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: With spill restrictions gone and terminals staffed, the port says it can load as soon as the entrance opens. Storage is the clock the market is watching.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from Corpus Christi remained halted Tuesday, the 13th day since an explosion near the Port Aransas jetties closed the ship channel. The port said it is ready to load as soon as the entrance reopens.

"Berths are clear and terminals are staffed," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "The plan for the first days is written. We need the entrance."

Navy and Coast Guard teams are still searching the channel after finding and making safe a second explosive device Friday. Neither service has given a completion date.

The situation differs from the storm closure in one respect that favors a faster recovery. Restrictions on the inner channel, imposed for decontamination after the September oil spill, were lifted the day the entrance closed. When ships can enter again, every berth will be available at full speed.

It differs in another respect that does not. "In September the tanks started with room," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "This time they started half recovered from the last closure. There is less cushion."

Holloway said she still had no evidence of producers cutting output because of the halt. She said that would be the next thing to watch if the closure ran well past two weeks. "Storage buys time. It has bought two weeks. I would not want to promise a month," she said.

The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports.

Some buyers have again turned to other Gulf Coast ports, as they did during the storm closure. Holloway said the pattern is becoming familiar. "The first time, people improvised. The second time, they had the phone numbers," she said. "Some of that business will be slower to come back."

Ships continue to hold at the offshore anchorage.

The Coast Guard said there was no change in port condition.

item.title: Corpus Christi export halt reaches 12th day as entrance sweep continues
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: A second explosive device found Friday has pushed back hopes for a quick restart. An analyst says buyers are now planning around the halt rather than waiting it out.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi remained halted Monday, the 12th day since an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties closed the ship channel.

Navy teams found a second explosive device near the entrance channel Friday and rendered it safe. The Navy and Coast Guard have said the search will continue until it is complete and have given no reopening date.

The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports, analysts say, making the closure the most significant disruption to U.S. export flows since Hurricane Rafael shut the channel in September.

"Last week, buyers were waiting. This week, they're planning around it," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The second device told everyone this isn't a matter of days. Nobody knows if it's weeks. When you don't know, you start booking alternatives, and some of that business may not come straight back."

Holloway said storage in the Corpus Christi area was absorbing crude that would normally have shipped, but that the cushion is finite. "Tanks fill. At some point, the barrels upstream have to slow down too," she said.

Market participants are watching for three signals: a Coast Guard notice changing the port's condition, an announced order for vessel movements once the channel opens, and any statement on how long a full restart would take after two closures in two months.

The Navy has attributed the Oct. 28 blast to an explosive device, and the FBI is investigating.

item.title: Week ahead: Corpus Christi closure enters a second full week with the market asking who signs off
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: A storm closure ends with a survey. This one ends when the Navy and Coast Guard say the channel is clear, and owners and insurers will want that in writing.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed for 11 days. Navy teams found and made safe a second explosive device Friday, and the search of the channel continues. Crude exports are halted.

The question for the week is not only when the Coast Guard lifts its order but what owners, charterers and insurers will need to see before they act on it.

"The reopening notice is one document," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The decision to send a ship is another, and somebody's underwriter is in that conversation."

Holloway said she had no information on any change in insurance terms for ships calling at Corpus Christi. Her point was about process. After a hurricane, a channel survey measures depths and checks buoys, and the industry knows how to read the result. After explosive devices, the assurance has to come from the Navy and the Coast Guard, and it rests on their judgment.

"That is not a criticism. It is the only way it can work. But the market is not used to it at a U.S. crude port," she said.

Ian McCready, an independent maritime security analyst and former Coast Guard watchstander, said outside data cannot shorten the wait. "There is nothing in a tracking feed that tells you a channel is clean. The people in the water tell you that," he said. McCready was among analysts who noted Monday that a spoofed vessel identity had appeared near the entrance two weeks before the blast. Officials have not commented on any link.

At the offshore anchorage, ships are still holding. Holloway said that reflects cost as much as confidence. "Leaving has a price too. A ship that sails for another port gives up its place here."

What to watch: any Navy statement on the progress of the search; any Coast Guard change in port condition; and whether ships begin leaving the anchorage in numbers.

The FBI investigation continues.

item.title: Second explosive device found near Corpus Christi entrance; crude export halt extends
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Navy teams rendered the device safe. The find ends any expectation of a quick restart, on the ninth day of the closure.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Navy teams found a second explosive device near the entrance channel at Corpus Christi on Friday and rendered it safe, the Navy said, extending a crude export halt now in its ninth day.

"Navy explosive ordnance disposal personnel located a second device near the entrance channel and rendered it safe," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. "The search continues. I will not describe the device."

The ship channel has been closed since an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties on Oct. 28. The Navy attributed that blast to an explosive device. The FBI is investigating.

The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports. No loadings have taken place since the closure.

"One device, you can tell yourself it was the only one," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Two, and the question becomes how many. That is a different kind of search and a different kind of wait."

Holloway said buyers who had held ships at the offshore anchorage in the hope of a short closure would now reconsider. "Yesterday you could argue for waiting. Today the people paying for those ships are going to ask for a plan," she said.

She said the find is not, by itself, bad news for the eventual restart. "You want them finding things. A search that finds nothing after one blast leaves people wondering. But it tells you the calendar is not days."

The Navy and Coast Guard have not said how much of the channel has been searched or how long the remaining work will take.

Storage along the channel is filling for the second time this fall. Unlike in September, terminals, power and city services are all working, and inner-channel spill restrictions were lifted last week. The only constraint on exports is the entrance.

The Coast Guard said the closure order remains in effect.

item.title: Two variables for crude: a crisis abroad and a closed channel at home
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: An overseas power has begun military operations, and its state broadcaster is mocking the Corpus Christi closure. An analyst says the market is pricing both and understands neither.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The crude market is working through two disruptions at once this week: a crisis abroad that escalated when an overseas power began military operations, and the continued closure of the U.S. port that handles about half of the country's crude exports.

The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed for seven days, since an explosion beside a harbor tug near the entrance. The Navy has said an explosive device caused it and is searching the channel with the Coast Guard. No reopening date has been set.

"Either one alone is a story," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Together they are a week nobody wants to trade."

Holloway said the two events pull on the market in the same direction. A crisis abroad raises concern about supply from other regions. A closed Corpus Christi removes the largest outlet for U.S. crude that might otherwise fill a gap. "The barrels exist. They are in tanks in Texas. They cannot get to a ship," she said.

A foreign state broadcaster has mocked the port closure in its coverage, presenting it as a sign of American weakness. Holloway said traders should treat that as noise. "State television is not a market signal. The Coast Guard's notice is the market signal," she said.

U.S. officials have not connected the explosion to events abroad, and Sabal has no information that they are related.

What the market does not know is how long either disruption lasts. Holloway said that uncertainty, more than the lost volume so far, is what participants are reacting to. "A week of Corpus Christi is absorbable. We saw a month of it in September and October and the system bent without breaking. What is different is that nobody can describe the end of this one," she said.

Storage along the ship channel, drawn down since the October reopening, is filling again.

The FBI is investigating the explosion.

item.title: Corpus Christi crude loadings stay halted as channel search continues
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The second export stoppage since Hurricane Rafael has no end date. An analyst says there is no substitute route at the port's scale.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi remained halted Tuesday as Navy teams continued searching the ship channel after the Oct. 28 explosion near the Port Aransas jetties, with no reopening date announced.

The halt is the port's second since Hurricane Rafael. Exports stopped when the Coast Guard closed the channel ahead of the storm in September and resumed only after a partial reopening in mid-October, when a backlog of vessels was still working through the offshore anchorage.

Analysts estimate the port moves about half of all U.S. crude exports. The Navy said Saturday that the blast beside a harbor tug was caused by an explosive device.

"There isn't a second door at this scale," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Every day the channel stays shut, barrels that would have left Corpus Christi either sit in tanks or wait for a ship that can't get in. You can move some volume elsewhere along the coast, but not all of it, and not quickly."

Holloway said the market's main question had shifted from damage to duration. "After the storm, people were asking what broke. Now they are asking how long a search takes, and nobody will give them a number. That's the right answer for safety. It's a hard answer for a cargo schedule."

Tankers that would normally queue at the offshore anchorage are holding as they wait for the channel to reopen. Buyers with cargoes booked from the port are weighing whether to wait or seek supply elsewhere, Holloway said.

The Coast Guard has not given a timeline. Officials have said the channel will reopen when it is safe.

item.title: Analysts flag spoofed vessel identity near Corpus Christi entrance two weeks before blast; crude buyers ask what else is unknown
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Officials decline to comment on any link. For the market, the question is no longer only when the channel reopens but what it would take to trust it.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Maritime analysts say a spoofed vessel identity appeared near the Corpus Christi entrance channel two weeks before the explosion that closed it, adding to the questions crude buyers are asking as the export halt enters its fifth day.

Public vessel-tracking data showed the identity of the fishing vessel FV Pelican Ridge broadcasting off Port Aransas overnight Oct. 14 to Oct. 15, while the same vessel reported a position about 600 nautical miles away. Analysts described that at the time as consistent with identity spoofing.

"I can tell you where the signal was. I cannot tell you what it means," said Ian McCready, an independent maritime security analyst and former Coast Guard watchstander. "It was near the entrance. That is a fact from public data. Anything past that is for investigators."

Officials declined to comment on any link to the blast.

The Navy has said an explosive device caused the explosion beside a harbor tug near the jetties Oct. 28. Navy teams are searching the channel with the Coast Guard, and the FBI is investigating. Crude exports from the port, about half of the U.S. total, are halted.

"After the storm the question was when," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Now there is a second question, which is whether. Whether the entrance is clear, and whether anyone can say so with confidence."

Holloway said that changes how buyers think about the closure. A storm closure ends when the weather and the survey allow. A security closure ends when authorities are satisfied, and that standard is harder to forecast.

She said she expected owners and insurers to ask more questions before sending ships back, though she had no information on any change in terms. "People will want to hear the Navy say the word clear," she said.

The Coast Guard has given no reopening date.

item.title: FBI: GPS interference traced to transmitter in vehicle parked near Inner Harbor fuel terminal
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The interference that pilots reported near Corpus Christi has stopped. Investigators found its source in an industrial area off the Inner Harbor, in a week when the ship channel is closed for another reason.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The FBI said Sunday that investigators had traced the GPS interference reported by pilots near Corpus Christi to a transmitter found in a parked vehicle in an industrial area near a fuel terminal off the Inner Harbor.

"Investigators traced the interference to a transmitter located in a parked vehicle," said Mark Ellery, a spokesman for the FBI's Houston Division. "The investigation is ongoing. We will not discuss evidence."

Ellery did not name the terminal or say who owned the vehicle.

Pilots had reported interference within about 40 miles of the city, and the Federal Aviation Administration issued a notice. "Those reports have stopped," said Lynn Carver, a regional spokesperson for the FAA.

The disclosure adds another unexplained security event to an energy corridor that has had several this fall.

The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed since Thursday, when an explosion went off beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties. The Navy said Saturday that an explosive device caused it, and Navy teams are searching the channel with the Coast Guard. The FBI is investigating that as well. Crude exports are halted for the second time in two months.

No agency has said the interference and the explosion are connected. Ellery declined to answer when asked.

A security director at one area energy company, who asked not to be named, said firms along the Inner Harbor had been asked this weekend to review vehicles parked on or near their property. "You check your fence line every day. You don't usually check the street," he said.

Fuel terminals, like crude docks and refineries, are regulated for physical security at their gates and waterfronts. Radio interference from outside the fence is not something those plans typically address.

The FBI did not say when the vehicle was found.

Sabal will report further findings as they are released.

item.title: Corpus Christi crude exports halted again; traders brace for a long closure
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The Navy's confirmation of an explosive device and an active channel search leave the timeline open. Traders are watching for a prolonged closure.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from the Port of Corpus Christi are halted again after the Navy said Saturday that an explosive device caused Thursday's blast beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties. Navy teams are searching the ship channel with the Coast Guard.

It is the second halt in two months at the port, which handles about half of U.S. crude exports. The first began when the Coast Guard closed the port to inbound ships two days before Hurricane Rafael's Sept. 14 landfall; the channel partly reopened Oct. 14.

"Once you hear 'explosive device' and 'search,' you stop modeling days," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "A search has to finish before anyone signs off on the channel, and nobody is going to rush that. I'd tell buyers to plan around weeks."

Traders are watching for a prolonged closure. Neither the Coast Guard nor the Navy has given a timeline for reopening, and the FBI is investigating the blast.

Holloway said the timing compounds the storm's disruption, with cargoes that had only begun moving again after Rafael back on hold. "Corpus Christi spent a month shut by one shock," she said. "It got two weeks of traffic before the next."

Before Rafael, the port had been loading crude tankers at a near-record pace, with exports reaching a monthly high two weeks before the storm. "Whatever ground the partial reopening won back is gone for now," Holloway said.

Sabal Energy Wire will track Coast Guard and Navy statements for any change in the channel's status.

item.title: EXCLUSIVE: Documents show Corpus Christi utility outages caused in part by deliberate control system manipulation predating the storm
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Documents obtained by Sabal Energy Wire confirm that the prolonged power outages affecting portions of Corpus Christi were caused not solely by hurricane damage but by deliberate manipulation of utility control systems — with relay configuration files bearing modification timestamps predating Hurricane Rafael's landfall by as much as 72 hours.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Documents obtained by Sabal Energy Wire confirm that the extended power outages that left thousands of Corpus Christi residents without electricity for as long as 35 days following Hurricane Rafael were caused not solely by hurricane damage but by deliberate manipulation of the utility's control systems — and that evidence of that manipulation was present in configuration files dating back as far as 72 hours before the storm made landfall.

The documents, which Sabal Energy Wire is not reproducing in full given the sensitivity of the ongoing federal investigation, include internal configuration records from Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority's electrical protection and relay systems. Those records show modification timestamps predating Hurricane Rafael's Sept. 14 landfall by approximately 72 hours. The nature of the modifications, as reflected in the documents, affected the operational parameters of protective relay equipment responsible for automatic switching and load management in the utility's distribution system. Industry engineers who reviewed the documents with Sabal Energy Wire said the modifications would have caused or worsened switching failures that the utility publicly attributed to storm damage during the initial days of the outage.

"These documents confirm that the prolonged power outages affecting portions of Corpus Christi were caused by deliberate manipulation of utility control systems, not solely by hurricane damage," one source familiar with the investigation said, speaking on condition of anonymity because the federal investigation is ongoing. "Relay configuration files show modification timestamps predating the storm." The source did not characterize who made the modifications or at whose direction, citing the investigation. Sabal Energy Wire was unable to independently verify the modification history through a second set of documents, and the account relies on the described documents and the source's characterization of them.

CBPWA declined to comment on the documents when contacted Friday. The authority has consistently said it cannot discuss details of the federal investigation. CISA, the FBI, and the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Texas all declined to comment. The governor's amended disaster declaration, signed Oct. 12, referenced the utility's operational technology systems being isolated as a precautionary measure; CBPWA and CISA confirmed on Oct. 20 that the utility's systems had been cleaned, rebuilt, and reconnected following a comprehensive security audit.

If the documents' content is confirmed through the federal process, what it would add to the record is timing. Federal officials and CBPWA said on Oct. 5 that the outages were prolonged by deliberate interference with control systems; the documents indicate the changes were in place before the storm arrived, which would mean the interference was planned ahead of the hurricane rather than improvised after it. The relay issues that caused the final 3,200 customers to remain without power until Oct. 19 were attributed by CBPWA to relay inspection and hardening work, without reference to external manipulation. Sabal Energy Wire will continue to report on this investigation as new information becomes available.

item.title: Corpus Christi crude exports stall again as Coast Guard shuts channel after blast
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Tanker traffic at the top U.S. crude export port stopped two weeks after a partial reopening. Analysts say duration is the key unknown.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Tanker traffic at the Port of Corpus Christi stopped again Thursday after the Coast Guard closed the ship channel following an overnight explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties.

The closure comes two weeks after the channel partly reopened from Hurricane Rafael, which shut the port for a month. Exports first halted when the port closed to inbound ships two days before the Sept. 14 landfall. Before the storm, the port was loading crude tankers at a near-record pace, and it handles about half of U.S. crude exports.

"Two weeks ago, the question was how fast the inner channel could clear decontamination. Today the question is whether anything moves at all," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Duration is everything. A closure of days is a scheduling problem. A closure of weeks is a supply problem for buyers who were already short."

The Coast Guard said the tug, the Corrin Bay, was damaged and two crew members were injured. Officials said the cause is unknown and gave no estimate for reopening.

In a twist of timing, the Unified Command overseeing the Inner Harbor spill said Thursday that cleanup was moving to monitoring and lifted the inner-channel restrictions that had constrained traffic since the partial reopening. "That would have been the good-news headline," Holloway said. "Instead, it's a footnote."

Holloway said market participants will be watching Coast Guard notices closely in the coming days. "Nobody's pricing a reopening until the Coast Guard says what happened," she said. "Until then, every cargo scheduled out of Corpus Christi is a question mark."

item.title: Last boil-water notice lifted in Corpus Christi; water plant back at full capacity
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Districts 3 and 4 were the final areas under notice. The city says pressure and testing now meet state standards, closing out the utility's storm recovery.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The boil-water notice for Corpus Christi's Districts 3 and 4 was lifted Tuesday, ending the last water restriction in the city six weeks after Hurricane Rafael.

The city said water pressure across the affected zone had been confirmed above 40 psi at all test points and that water quality testing met state standards. The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant is operating at full capacity, it said.

"You can drink the water," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokeswoman for the city water utility. "Thank you for boiling it for as long as you did. We know what we asked of you."

The citywide notice was lifted Saturday after replacement pump parts were installed and tested. Districts 3 and 4, where low pressure had prompted a separate notice in late September, stayed under restriction until Tuesday.

The plant lost both power feeds early in the storm and ran for weeks on temporary pumps while replacement parts, delayed when the supplier's local warehouse flooded, shipped from out of state.

For industry along the ship channel, the announcement closes the utility chapter of the recovery. Power was fully restored last week, and Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority has said its control systems have returned to normal monitoring after a security incident that federal agencies are still investigating.

"That leaves the water the ships float in," said a shipping agent who asked not to be named because he was not authorized to speak for his principals. He was referring to the inner channel, where spill decontamination still restricts traffic.

The ship channel partly reopened Oct. 14. Crude loadings have resumed below the pre-storm pace.

Gallegos said residents who still see discolored water should run their taps for several minutes and call the utility if it does not clear.

The city has not yet said what permanent repairs or upgrades it plans at the plant. Gallegos said that review would come after the emergency work was complete.

item.title: Week ahead: Corpus Christi waits on inner-channel limits as city services return
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The citywide boil-water notice is lifted and power is back. On the water, decontamination still restricts the inner channel, and pilots in the air have reported GPS interference.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Ten days after the Corpus Christi Ship Channel partly reopened, the city around the port is closer to normal than the port itself.

City services. The citywide boil-water notice was lifted Saturday after pump repairs and testing at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant. Districts 3 and 4 remain under a separate notice. Power has been restored to the last customers.

The channel. Spill decontamination continues to restrict the inner channel. Crude loadings are running below the pre-storm pace and the backlog at the offshore anchorage is working down slowly.

"The city is nearly back. The port is half back," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The half that is missing is the inner channel."

Holloway said the timing of that last step is the main variable for crude flows this week. The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports in normal operation. "When those restrictions lift, every berth turns ships at full speed again. Until then the anchorage empties slower than it fills," she said.

A new item. Pilots have reported GPS interference within about 40 miles of Corpus Christi, and the Federal Aviation Administration has issued a notice. Relief flights into the area are continuing on backup navigation.

The notice is addressed to aviation and no agency has reported any effect on shipping. Holloway said the market had not reacted. "It is on my list because it is unexplained and it is here. That is all I can say about it," she said.

Storage along the channel is drawing down as cargoes load. Holloway said some buyers who diverted to other Gulf ports during the closure have begun asking about Corpus Christi slots for November.

What to watch: a Coast Guard notice lifting the inner-channel restrictions; the Unified Command's status for the spill cleanup; the remaining boil-water notice; and any explanation of the interference.

"If the restrictions come off this week, the conversation in November is about volume again," Holloway said.

item.title: Corpus Christi utilities clear three hurdles in two days: power, control systems and pump parts
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The last customers have power, the utility says its control-system cleanup has finished an initial phase, and replacement pump parts have reached the water plant.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Corpus Christi's utilities cleared three recovery milestones this week, five weeks after Hurricane Rafael.

Power. Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority said Tuesday that the final 3,200 customers in northwest Corpus Christi had been restored after relay inspection, repair and hardening work. All load zones are above 99 percent restoration, the utility said.

Control systems. CBPWA and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said Wednesday that the utility had completed an initial phase of remediation after a confirmed security incident affecting its industrial control system network. Security monitoring has returned to normal status and no customer data was taken, they said. CISA issued an advisory to other infrastructure operators on the techniques observed.

Water. Replacement parts for the damaged pumps at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant arrived Wednesday. They had been delayed after the supplier's local warehouse flooded and the order had to ship from out of state.

"The parts are here," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokeswoman for the city water utility. "Now we install them and test, and the boil-water notice stays until the tests pass. We are close. Please stay with us a little longer."

The three updates matter to the energy sector because the port's restart depends on the city around it. The ship channel partly reopened last week, and crude loadings have resumed at a reduced pace while spill decontamination restricts the inner channel.

A terminal manager, who asked not to be named because he was not authorized to speak for his company, said the power restoration mattered most to his workforce. "My operators have been running a dock all day and going home to a generator," he said. "That ended this week for the last of them."

CBPWA said it is conducting a post-incident review and will add security measures identified in the investigation. Federal investigators have not attributed the intrusion.

The utility has not set a date for lifting the boil-water notice.

item.title: CBPWA and CISA declare utility's OT systems clean and secure; enhanced monitoring now active
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: A joint statement Wednesday confirmed that Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority's operational technology network has been cleaned, rebuilt, and reconnected after a comprehensive security audit — marking the formal close of the period of full manual operations that began when systems were isolated.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued a joint statement Wednesday confirming that the utility's operational technology systems have been cleaned, rebuilt, and reconnected to operational use following a comprehensive security audit. The announcement ends the period of fully manual utility operations that began when the authority isolated its OT network under federal guidance in the days after the Oct. 5 disclosure of the utility cyberattack.

"CBPWA and CISA have confirmed that the utility's operational technology systems have been cleaned, rebuilt and reconnected," the joint statement reads. "A comprehensive security audit is complete. The utility has implemented enhanced monitoring and access controls." The statement does not describe the specific nature of the modifications found or made during the audit, citing the ongoing federal investigation.

The reconnection marks a significant operational milestone for the authority's field crews, who have been managing all water treatment, distribution, and electrical switching functions manually for more than a week. Manual operations in a system of CBPWA's scale — serving more than 300,000 residents across Corpus Christi and the surrounding county — requires substantially larger crews and extends the time required for routine tasks. Industry sources said the authority brought in contracted crews during the manual period to maintain service standards.

The enhanced monitoring referenced in the statement reflects new ICS security architecture that CISA and the authority declined to detail publicly, citing security sensitivity. Industry experts familiar with post-incident OT recovery said that rebuilt systems typically include enhanced logging, network segmentation, and privileged access management controls that did not exist in the original configuration. CISA's ED 27-02, issued Oct. 7, required all federal ICS operators to audit remote-access credentials; Wednesday's statement suggests CBPWA's own audit and remediation work has concluded.

The authority said the boil-water notice for Districts 3 and 4 remains in effect separately from the OT systems status and is awaiting full pressure normalization and sampling clearance across the two districts. The boil-water notice and the OT reconnection are distinct milestones, the authority said, and the water advisory will not be lifted until the water system independently meets state and federal testing standards.

item.title: CBPWA restores power to final 3,200 customers, completing 35-day recovery from Rafael damage
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Field crews completed manual power restoration procedures overnight Tuesday, bringing all Corpus Christi load zones above 99 percent restored — but the milestone comes after relay inspection and hardening work that exposed infrastructure vulnerabilities beyond what hurricane damage alone would explain.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority field crews completed manual power restoration procedures overnight Monday into Tuesday, restoring service to the final 3,200 customers who have been without power since Hurricane Rafael made landfall 35 days ago. All Corpus Christi load zones are now above 99 percent restoration, the authority said in a statement Tuesday afternoon, citing the milestone as completion of the Rafael power restoration effort.

"Following relay inspection and hardening work at two facilities, field crews completed manual restoration procedures overnight," the CBPWA statement reads. "All Corpus Christi load zones are now above 99 percent restoration following Hurricane Rafael." The authority noted that the final phase of restoration required manual protocols because its operational technology systems remain isolated under guidance from CISA and federal investigators. No date has been given for reconnecting automated control systems.

The 35-day restoration timeline is significantly longer than typical post-hurricane power recovery for a storm of Rafael's intensity, and the relay inspection work mentioned in Tuesday's statement has drawn attention from the utility industry and from regulators. Industry engineers familiar with the recovery noted that relay hardening is not standard hurricane restoration work. Protective relays are normally factory-configured and require modification only under specific technical circumstances; a relay configuration issue is what the federal investigation has identified as connected to the unauthorized SCADA access disclosed Oct. 5.

CBPWA did not answer questions about the specific nature of the relay findings or their relationship to the federal investigation. The authority said the two facilities where hardening work was required have been restored to service and that all relay configurations have been reviewed and verified. The authority declined to name the facilities.

For the 3,200 customers who endured the final stretch of the outage — many of them in the Hillcrest and Oak Park neighborhoods where utility infrastructure sustained damage during and after the storm surge — Tuesday marked the end of a period that in some cases included extended stays at family homes, shelters, or hotels. The CBPWA statement thanked those customers for their patience and noted that all utility bills would reflect applicable outage credits per state PUC guidelines.

item.title: Corpus Christi crude loadings restart at reduced pace as inner-channel limits and backlog slow recovery
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Two days into the partial reopening, ships are moving again. Spill decontamination still restricts the inner channel, and the line at the anchorage is weeks deep.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude loadings at Corpus Christi have restarted at a reduced pace two days after the ship channel partly reopened, with spill decontamination still restricting the inner channel and a backlog of ships waiting offshore.

The Coast Guard partly reopened the channel Thursday, a month after it closed ahead of Hurricane Rafael. The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports.

"Ships are moving. Not as many as we want, and not as fast," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "The inner channel is still under restrictions for decontamination, and we have a long line at the anchorage. We are working it one ship at a time."

The backlog is delaying all kinds of cargo, including relief shipments that have been waiting since before the storm.

"Open is not the same as normal," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The market got the first word this week. It is still waiting for the second."

Holloway said three things are holding the pace down. Transits are being sequenced carefully after a month with no deep-draft traffic. Berths in the restricted inner reach turn ships more slowly because of decontamination. And the queue offshore includes ships that have waited for weeks alongside new arrivals.

She would not estimate how long it would take to return to the pre-storm loading rate. "It depends on when the inner-channel restrictions come off. Until then you have a port working with one hand," she said.

Storage along the channel, which absorbed a month of crude that could not ship, will start to draw down as tankers load, she said. "That is the pressure valve opening. It does not open all at once."

Buyers who diverted to other Gulf ports during the closure are not expected to return immediately. "People who made other arrangements will finish them," Holloway said.

The Coast Guard has not said when the remaining restrictions will be lifted.

item.title: Corpus Christi partial reopening leaves crude market watching inner-channel limits
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The Coast Guard eased the storm closure at the largest U.S. crude export gateway, but spill decontamination still restricts the inner channel and an anchorage backlog sets the pace.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The Coast Guard partly reopened the Corpus Christi Ship Channel on Thursday, a month after Hurricane Rafael shut the port that handles about half of U.S. crude exports.

The reopening is partial. Spill decontamination keeps the inner channel restricted, according to the Coast Guard, and vessels are queued at the offshore anchorage. Exports halted when the port closed to inbound traffic two days before the Sept. 14 landfall, with 14 vessels waiting offshore at the time.

"Partial is the operative word," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The market cares less about the headline than about how many transits the inner channel can handle under decontamination rules. Until that's clear, nobody should model a quick return to pre-storm volumes."

Before Rafael, the port was loading crude tankers at a near-record pace, with tankers routinely waiting their turn at the offshore anchorage, and exports hit a monthly high two weeks before the storm.

Holloway said buyers who had been counting on Corpus Christi barrels over the past month have had to adjust, and that the anchorage queue will need to clear before loadings settle into a rhythm. "You don't flip a switch on a port this size," she said. "You work the queue."

Port officials have not given a date for lifting the inner-channel restriction. The port said the backlog is also delaying relief cargo, including the cargo ship MV Gulf Provider.

Market participants will be watching Coast Guard notices for any change to the restriction in the days ahead, Holloway said, along with the pace at which the anchorage line shortens.

item.title: CBPWA isolates operational technology network under CISA guidance; crews shift to fully manual operations
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority confirmed Wednesday that it has taken precautionary steps to isolate portions of its operational technology network, placing all utility control functions under manual field management as federal cybersecurity experts assess the systems.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority confirmed Wednesday that it has isolated portions of its operational technology network as a precautionary measure, acting under guidance from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. The isolation means all control functions for the authority's water treatment, distribution and electrical systems are now managed by field crews without automated assistance from the utility's SCADA infrastructure.
