"CBPWA has taken precautionary steps to isolate portions of its operational technology network under guidance from CISA," the authority said in a statement released Wednesday afternoon. "Field crews are managing operations manually during this period. Restoration of electric service continues on manual protocols. The water supply remains safe for boiled use in Districts 3 and 4." The authority did not indicate when it expected to restore automated operations.

Manual operations represent a significant burden on field crews, who must make and execute control decisions that would ordinarily be handled or assisted by automated systems. Sources familiar with utility operations said manual management of a water and power system serving roughly 500,000 people requires substantial additional staffing and extends the time needed for routine tasks including load balancing, pressure adjustments, and switching. The authority has not addressed publicly whether it has contracted additional crews for the manual operations period.

The network isolation was first indicated in the governor's amended disaster declaration signed Tuesday, which noted that the utility had isolated its control systems as a precautionary measure. Wednesday's statement from CBPWA is the authority's first direct public confirmation. A FEMA-deployed cybersecurity rapid response team is on-site working alongside state and federal investigators. The underlying federal investigation into the unauthorized SCADA access remains ongoing.

For utility industry observers, the combination of network isolation, manual operations and federal team deployment marks a significant response posture. CISA has not publicly described the scope of the OT isolation or what assessment activities are underway. The authority said it would provide updates as the situation developed and that its first priority remained maintaining safe and adequate utility service to all customers.

item.title: Corpus Christi channel closure passes one month; port says it is ready when the Coast Guard is
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Crude exports from the nation's largest crude export port have been halted since Sept. 12. Port officials say berths and terminals will move as soon as the Coast Guard clears the channel.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — A month after the Coast Guard shut the Corpus Christi Ship Channel ahead of Hurricane Rafael, crude exports from the Port of Corpus Christi were still halted Wednesday.

The port, which handles about half of U.S. crude exports according to analysts' estimates, has had no export traffic through the channel since Sept. 12. At the anchorage east of Port Aransas, 14 vessels were waiting when the port closed to inbound ships that day.

"We are ready when the Coast Guard is," port spokesperson Javier Salinas said. "Our job is to have berths, pilots and terminals lined up so the minute the channel opens, ships move. That work is happening now."

Salinas declined to give a reopening date, noting that port conditions are set by the Coast Guard, which has said the channel will reopen when it is safe for traffic. Spill response continues in the Inner Harbor and the bays, where about 9,000 barrels released by two moored tankers spread across about 33 square miles after the storm.

Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics, said traders are focused on what comes after the reopening as much as on the reopening itself. "The first day isn't the story. The story is how fast the backlog clears," she said. "You've got ships that have been waiting offshore and buyers who have been sourcing elsewhere for a month. It will take time to get back to rhythm."

Holloway said the Coast Guard's investigation into possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo systems of the two tankers is also on traders' minds. "Nobody's pricing it in yet," she said. "But everyone's asking their own terminals what's connected to what."

The Coast Guard has not announced when the channel will reopen.

item.title: Texas adds cyber emergency to Rafael disaster declaration; Corpus Christi utility running control systems by hand
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The governor's amendment covers Corpus Christi utility infrastructure. FEMA has sent a cybersecurity rapid response team, and field crews are managing operations manually.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The governor of Texas amended the Hurricane Rafael disaster declaration Tuesday to add a cyber emergency component covering Corpus Christi utility infrastructure, the governor's office said.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency has deployed a cybersecurity rapid response team to assist local and state authorities. The affected utility has isolated its control systems as a precaution, and field crews are managing operations manually, the statement said.

The governor's office said the water supply remains safe when boiled and that electric restoration is continuing.

The amendment is the latest step in a sequence that began when the FBI and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency confirmed they were investigating unauthorized access to control systems at a Corpus Christi utility. CISA followed with an emergency directive on remote-access audits. No attribution has been made.

For energy markets, the practical question is whether a utility running by hand can support an industrial restart.

"I cover crude. This month I am reading utility notices, because the port does not restart on crude alone," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics.

Holloway said manual operation is slower and more labor-intensive but is something utilities train for. "Operators ran grids and water systems by hand for a century. It works. It does not scale well, and it leaves no margin if something else goes wrong," she said.

She said she had no information that the isolation had interrupted service to any terminal or refinery. The Corpus Christi Ship Channel remains closed by the Coast Guard for reasons unrelated to the utility, and crude exports have been halted for a month.

The declaration's wording matters for cost recovery, she said. Adding a cyber component can open federal assistance for response work that a storm declaration alone would not cover.

The utility has not said how long its control systems will remain isolated.

item.title: Week ahead: Corpus Christi begins a fifth week shut, with parts, audits and a survey outstanding
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Pump parts for the water plant are shipping from out of state, a federal directive has operators auditing remote access, and the channel survey has no public end date.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Corpus Christi starts a fifth week without crude exports. The list of what stands between the port and a restart is shorter than it was, but three items are outstanding.

The channel. Still closed by the Coast Guard. The main oil slick has been contained, which removes one obstacle. The survey of the channel and the conditions for a first reopening have not been announced. Ships are waiting at the offshore anchorage.

The water plant. Replacement parts for the damaged pumps at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant are delayed. The utility said the supplier's local warehouse flooded and the parts are shipping from out of state. Temporary pumps continue to limit capacity, and boil-water notices remain.

The audits. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued an emergency directive Thursday requiring federal agencies that run industrial control systems to audit remote-access credentials and configuration change logs within 72 hours. It strongly encouraged private owners of critical infrastructure to review the same. The directive followed a confirmed incident at a Texas utility.

"Every one of these has a version of the same answer," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "In progress, no date."

Holloway said the audits are unlikely to delay a restart directly. "Checking who can log in to your systems does not stop you loading a ship. Finding something might," she said.

She said the pump parts matter mostly as a measure of the city's general recovery. "A supplier whose own warehouse flooded is the whole story of this month in one sentence."

On the channel, she said traders have begun to plan around a staged reopening without knowing when it starts. "People are asking terminals about slots. Terminals are saying, ask the Coast Guard."

What to watch: any Coast Guard notice on port condition; the utility's restoration and repair updates; and whether more operators disclose findings from their access reviews.

item.title: Slick containment removes one obstacle to a Corpus Christi restart; the channel decision remains
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Unified Command says the main slick is contained and primary skimming is finished. The fishing closure has been extended, and the Coast Guard still has not set a date.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The main oil slick from the Corpus Christi Inner Harbor spill has been contained and primary skimming is finished, the Unified Command has said, removing one of the obstacles to reopening the ship channel.

The announcement does not reopen it. The Coast Guard has kept the channel closed while it is surveyed and the spill is contained, and has not set a date. Ships remain at the offshore anchorage.

"This is the first item to come off the list since the storm," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "It is not the last item."

The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports. Loadings have been halted for nearly four weeks.

The state has extended the closure of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays to fishing, a sign that officials still consider oil in the water a concern even as respiratory complaints near the shoreline ease.

"Containment is a milestone. It is not the finish," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "Shoreline work continues, and the fishing closure stays until the testing supports lifting it."

Holloway said the market should expect a staged reopening when it comes. "The Coast Guard does not usually go from closed to open. There are steps, with conditions. And any ship that has been through oiled water may need cleaning before it goes anywhere else," she said.

That last point could matter for the first weeks of loading, she said, because it would slow the turn of each ship at berths near the spill site.

Storage along the channel has absorbed the halt so far. Holloway said she continues to see no sign of producers reducing output because of it.

"What changed this week is that a restart moved from hypothetical to something people are scheduling around," she said. "Nobody has a date. But people have started asking terminals about slots."

item.title: CISA issues emergency directive requiring ICS credential audit at all federal facilities within 72 hours
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Emergency Directive 27-02, issued Thursday, cites a "confirmed ICS incident at a Texas utility" and requires federal agency operators of industrial control systems to audit remote-access logs and change credential configurations immediately.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued an emergency directive Thursday requiring all federal agencies that operate industrial control systems to audit remote-access credentials and configuration change logs within 72 hours. The directive, designated ED 27-02, cites a confirmed ICS incident at an unnamed Texas utility as the basis for the accelerated compliance window.

The directive arrives two days after Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority publicly disclosed that investigators had confirmed unauthorized access to its supervisory control and data acquisition systems. That disclosure, made jointly with CISA and the FBI, identified the incident as the first publicly confirmed cyberattack on a Texas water utility's operational technology infrastructure since federal reporting requirements were expanded under the America's Water Infrastructure Act. The utility cyberattack is now the subject of a federal investigation; no attribution has been made public.

"CISA is directing all federal agencies operating industrial control systems to audit remote-access credentials and configuration change logs within 72 hours, following a confirmed ICS incident at a Texas utility," the directive states. It further requires agencies to submit a summary of findings to CISA's Federal Emergency Management Group within 96 hours of issuance and to implement any identified credential remediation actions within seven days.

The directive applies specifically to agencies operating their own ICS environments, not to critical infrastructure owners and operators in the private sector, though CISA issued a companion advisory recommending the same audit steps for all operators of water and wastewater operational technology. The advisory describes the access vector exploited in the Texas incident in general terms — unauthorized remote access to a supervisory control network — without disclosing specific technical details the agency says could assist threat actors targeting similar systems.

Industry analysts noted that the 72-hour window is among the tightest CISA has imposed under its emergency directive authority, which was expanded following the Colonial Pipeline ransomware incident in 2021. "This directive reflects genuine urgency," said one ICS security consultant, who was not authorized to speak on the record about ongoing federal matters. "When CISA issues a 72-hour audit window and ties it to a named incident class, they are telling the sector that the threat model has changed." CISA has not indicated when ED 27-02 will expire or transition to a standard binding operational directive.

item.title: Texas energy operators told to review remote access after Corpus Christi utility intrusion
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The governor has directed all critical infrastructure operators in the state to check remote-access procedures and report anomalies to CISA. Terminals and pipelines along the coast are on the list.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Energy companies across Texas are reviewing how outside parties connect to their control systems after the governor directed all critical infrastructure operators in the state to check remote-access security procedures and report anomalies to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

The directive followed confirmation Tuesday that the FBI and CISA are investigating unauthorized access to control systems at a Corpus Christi utility during the Hurricane Rafael response. Texas Cyber Command has been activated to assist. Officials have released no operational details and made no attribution.

Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority said Monday that it was investigating anomalous access to its internal network systems and that there was no indication customer data had been affected.

The order reaches well beyond one utility. Refineries, pipelines, crude terminals and power generators all count as critical infrastructure, and most allow some form of remote connection for vendors or their own engineers.

"The first step is a list," said Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with CISA. "Who can connect from outside, to what, and when did they last do it? Remove what is not needed. Separate control systems from everything else. If something looks wrong, report it. We would rather hear about ten things that turn out to be nothing."

Tran declined to discuss the utility investigation.

It is the second remote-access inquiry in Corpus Christi in three weeks. The Coast Guard is examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of two tankers involved in the Inner Harbor oil spill. No agency has linked the two matters.

Several operators contacted by Sabal declined to comment on their own reviews. A compliance officer at one pipeline company, who asked not to be named, said the instruction was clear enough. "Nobody needs to be told twice this month," she said.

The Corpus Christi Ship Channel remains closed and crude exports halted.

item.title: What the Corpus Christi Utility Cyberattack Reveals About the Nation's Energy Infrastructure Vulnerabilities
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The confirmed cyberattack on Corpus Christi utility systems during Hurricane Rafael is precisely the scenario that energy security specialists have warned about for years — and its aftermath is likely to accelerate long-stalled federal mandates on operational technology security.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — When CISA and the FBI announced Tuesday that unauthorized actors had accessed and manipulated industrial control systems at a Corpus Christi utility during Hurricane Rafael, the energy sector did not need a press release to understand the significance. The scenario — a sophisticated actor targeting operational technology during a natural disaster, exploiting the chaos and reduced monitoring capacity of a major storm to mask deliberate infrastructure interference — is precisely what utility security specialists have warned about for years in classified briefings, red-team exercises, and academic literature.

CBPWA's Monday statement confirming an investigation into "anomalous access to operational technology systems" gave the energy sector a 36-hour window to begin assessing the implications before Tuesday's formal announcement. "What this appears to be is a timing attack," said Dr. Sara Okonkwo, director of the Critical Infrastructure Security Laboratory at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi. "You exploit a natural disaster's disruption of normal monitoring and response capacity to do something to a system that would otherwise be detected and responded to quickly. The storm gives you cover. The recovery chaos sustains it."

The specific systems affected have not been publicly described by CISA or the FBI. But the combination of events in Corpus Christi over the past three weeks — extended substation failures with anomalous relay conditions, water system pressure problems requiring a boil water notice, alongside an illness cluster that has sent more than 600 people to hospital, and a federal thermal survey that found breaker positions inconsistent with storm damage — suggests the attack, if confirmed as described, spanned multiple types of operational technology across both electric and water infrastructure. Energy sector analysts note that electric and water systems in mid-sized cities often share operational technology vendors and sometimes share network architecture.

The incident has already prompted an emergency security assessment bulletin from the North American Electric Reliability Corporation and an advisory from the Water Information Sharing and Analysis Center. Both organizations are asking member utilities to immediately audit remote access logs, review recent changes to programmable logic controller configurations, and ensure that operational technology networks are logically separated from information technology networks. Those basic hygiene measures, security specialists note, are requirements many utilities have not fully implemented despite years of federal guidance.

The broader question the Corpus Christi attack poses for energy policy is one that CISA has been trying to force for years: what is the obligation of the federal government, state regulators, and private utilities to harden operational technology against nation-state-level threats? The Rafael incident — in which an apparent attack amplified a natural disaster's impact on civilians, produced a public health emergency, and remained hidden beneath storm-damage narratives for three weeks — will almost certainly accelerate that conversation. "After today," said Dr. Okonkwo, "every utility in America that has not taken OT security seriously is going to have a very difficult time explaining to its regulators and its ratepayers why it hasn't."

item.title: CBPWA Confirms Probe into 'Anomalous Access' to Industrial Control Systems
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: In a terse Monday afternoon statement, the Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority has acknowledged for the first time that it is investigating unauthorized or anomalous access to its operational technology systems — a significant departure from the utility's previous storm-damage framing.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority issued a terse but significant statement Monday afternoon acknowledging that it is investigating anomalous access to portions of its operational technology systems — the first time the utility has used language that goes beyond storm-damage framing to describe the ongoing problems affecting its transmission and water distribution infrastructure. The statement was brief, carefully worded, and released at an hour that industry observers noted is unusual for utility communications.

"CBPWA has confirmed that it is investigating anomalous access to portions of its operational technology systems," CBPWA Communications Director Patricia Odom said in an emailed statement. "We are working with cybersecurity experts and have notified appropriate federal agencies. We want to assure customers that we are taking this matter with the utmost seriousness and that we are committed to transparency as this review proceeds." The statement did not name the federal agencies notified, describe the systems involved, characterize what kind of access occurred, or indicate how the access was discovered.

The statement is narrow and carefully worded. It does not say what was accessed, how the access occurred, or how long it lasted. It does not explicitly indicate whether the anomalous access is connected to the utility's power restoration challenges or to the boil water notice affecting Districts 3 and 4. CBPWA has until this point attributed all infrastructure problems to Hurricane Rafael's physical damage. The sudden departure from that framing — without additional explanation — has raised immediate questions among energy sector analysts and customers who have been without power or safe water for three weeks.

The timing of the statement struck energy sector observers as notable. "Utilities don't issue this kind of statement on a Monday afternoon unless they've been asked to by a federal agency, or unless they're getting ahead of something they know is coming," said one utility sector cybersecurity consultant who requested anonymity because they advise clients in the region. The Public Utility Commission of Texas and ERCOT, both of which have been monitoring CBPWA's restoration progress, did not comment Monday afternoon. Sabal Energy Wire will continue to report as this story develops. Residents in Districts 3 and 4 are asked to maintain current power and water conservation measures while the utility investigation continues.

item.title: Week ahead: three clocks running in Corpus Christi, and the grid's is the newest
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The channel survey, the spill response and now a power restoration that the utility says was set back by cascading substation failures.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Corpus Christi enters its fourth week without crude exports with three separate timelines in play. Two are familiar. The third became visible last week.

The channel. Closed by the Coast Guard while it is surveyed and the Inner Harbor oil spill is contained. Ships are waiting at the offshore anchorage. No date.

The spill. A claims center for the tankers' owners has opened. Fishing closures in the bays remain. The Coast Guard investigation into how oil left the two tankers continues.

The grid. Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority said Tuesday that restoration crews had encountered cascading substation failures in the northwest and central districts, extending the recovery beyond initial estimates. The utility said crews were at two facilities investigating protective relay conditions made worse by storm debris, and that it expected the final 32,000 affected customers to be restored within 7 to 10 days.

A federal aerial survey released Wednesday identified two CBPWA substations, Harbor View and Crosstown, as needing follow-up engineering inspection because of equipment configurations seen in the imagery.

"Two weeks ago I had the grid in the solved column. I have moved it back," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics.

Holloway said the areas named by the utility are not the ship channel itself, and she had no information that terminals lacked power. Her concern is pace. "A port restart needs people and services across the whole city. If a large part of town is still dark when the channel opens, the first week will be slower than the market assumes," she said.

The utility's 7-to-10-day window, counted from Tuesday, runs through the end of this week.

What to watch: CBPWA's restoration count, any finding from the substation inspections, and, as always, the Coast Guard.

"I would trade all three updates for one sentence from the Captain of the Port," Holloway said.

item.title: Explainer: what a closed ship channel means for Corpus Christi's refiners
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Exporters with no ships have no sales. Refiners have pipelines, trucks and tanks, which buys time but not indefinitely.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Nearly three weeks into the closure of the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, most attention has gone to crude exports, which stopped the day the port closed to inbound ships. The refineries along the Inner Harbor face a different problem.

Sabal described in August how exporters and refiners share one channel. This is what the closure means for the second group.

What still works. Pipelines. Much of the crude that feeds the area's refineries arrives by pipeline from inland, and much of the fuel they make leaves by pipeline and truck. None of that depends on the ship channel.

What does not. Anything that moves by water. Feedstock that normally arrives by ship or barge, and products that leave by tanker, cannot move while the channel is closed.

"An exporter is a tap. A refinery is a machine," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "You can shut a tap. A machine wants to keep running, and it needs somewhere to put what it makes."

Holloway said she had no information on the operating status of any individual plant, and the companies have not made public statements. Hurricane Rafael also brought widespread power outages and damage across the area, which would affect any industrial site regardless of the channel.

In general, she said, a refinery cut off from the water leans on storage and on its land routes. "Tanks are time. When product tanks fill, you slow down. That is true for any refinery anywhere."

Why the market cares. Corpus Christi's refineries supply fuel to Texas and beyond. Holloway said a long closure would show up first in the trade of products that normally leave by ship. "The crude export gap is the big number. The products gap is smaller and closer to home," she said.

The Coast Guard has kept the channel closed while it is surveyed and the Inner Harbor oil spill is contained. Ships are waiting at the offshore anchorage. No reopening date has been set.

item.title: Report of pre-storm drone flights over port and utility site adds a security question for energy operators
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Gulfwater Maritime Report says federal authorities are examining whether drones surveilled the Port of Corpus Christi and a power utility facility before Rafael. The FBI confirms only that it is investigating.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Federal authorities are examining whether commercial drones flew surveillance over the Port of Corpus Christi and at least one local power utility facility in the days before Hurricane Rafael, Gulfwater Maritime Report reported Thursday, citing sources familiar with the investigation.

The trade publication said the flights were detected through radar records maintained by the Coast Guard and took place in the week before landfall. No organization has claimed responsibility, it said.

Sabal has not independently confirmed the report.

"We can confirm the FBI is investigating reports of unauthorized drone activity in the Corpus Christi area," said Mark Ellery, a spokesman for the FBI's Houston Division. "We have no further comment." The FBI has asked the public for tips.

The Federal Aviation Administration and Customs and Border Protection said Wednesday that investigators had identified multiple incidents of unauthorized drone operations in the area in the period before the storm. They gave no locations.

For energy companies along the ship channel, the report lands in an already crowded security picture. The Coast Guard is examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of two tankers involved in the Inner Harbor oil spill.

No agency has said the drone flights are connected to the spill or to any storm damage, and the Gulfwater report did not say so.

A security manager at one area terminal, who asked not to be named because he was not authorized to speak publicly, said his company had been asked by federal investigators to preserve camera footage from early September. He declined to say more.

Terminals and refineries along the channel are subject to federal maritime security rules that require them to control access from land and water. Those rules were written with fences, gates and boats in mind.

The ship channel remains closed while it is surveyed and the spill is contained. Crude exports have been halted for nearly three weeks.

item.title: FEMA Thermal Survey Spots Anomalous Breaker Positions at Two Corpus Christi Substations
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: A federal aerial survey of post-Rafael utility damage has produced imagery showing breaker configurations at two substations that specialists say are difficult to attribute to storm mechanics alone, adding a new layer of uncertainty to Corpus Christi's stalled power recovery.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — A federal aerial survey of storm-damaged utility infrastructure in the Corpus Christi area has produced imagery showing anomalous circuit breaker configurations at two substations that have been at the center of ongoing power restoration delays, according to a FEMA Mitigation Assessment Team report released Wednesday. The findings are described in technical language in the publicly available document, but specialists who reviewed the report with Sabal Energy Wire say the anomalies are difficult to explain through storm mechanics alone.

FEMA's Mitigation Assessment Team conducted systematic post-storm overflights of utility infrastructure using UAS platforms equipped with thermal and optical sensors between September 23 and September 26. The report states that imagery of two substations — Harbor View and Crosstown — — Harbor View and Crosstown — — Harbor View and Crosstown — — Harbor View and Crosstown — — Harbor View and Crosstown — — Harbor View and Crosstown — — Harbor View and Crosstown — — Harbor View and Crosstown — — Harbor View and Crosstown — shows "breaker positions inconsistent with expected post-storm failure modes" and "thermal signatures at switching equipment warranting on-site evaluation." The report recommends that the utility's engineering staff review the flagged sites as a priority action.

CBPWA Communications Director Patricia Odom said the utility has received the FEMA report and is coordinating with its engineering teams on the findings. "We appreciate the federal team's systematic review," Odom said in an emailed statement. "We are evaluating all available data as part of our ongoing restoration work." She did not address whether the aerial findings had changed CBPWA's understanding of the relay failures flagged in Tuesday's operational statement, or whether CBPWA has requested outside forensic engineering assistance.

The FEMA Mitigation Assessment Team report is a standard post-disaster document produced to help utilities and local governments understand storm damage patterns and prioritize rebuilding. Officials from both FEMA and CBPWA emphasize that the report's characterization of "anomalous" breaker positions represents a technical observation, not a determination of cause, and that no federal agency has publicly attributed the substation conditions to anything other than the effects of Hurricane Rafael. The full report will be publicly posted to FEMA's website within ten business days, the agency said.

item.title: CBPWA Flags 'Cascading Substation Failures' as Rafael Power Recovery Stalls in Northwest Corpus Christi
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority has publicly acknowledged for the first time that failures at two substations are extending the recovery, and says the final 32,000 customers should be restored within 7 to 10 days.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority issued a rare operational statement Tuesday acknowledging that restoration crews working in northwest and central Corpus Christi have encountered what the utility described as "cascading substation failures" that are extending recovery timelines well beyond original projections. The statement marks the first time CBPWA has publicly acknowledged that something beyond routine storm damage is affecting two key transmission facilities.

"Restoration crews have encountered cascading substation failures in northwest and central Corpus Christi that are extending recovery," CBPWA Communications Director Patricia Odom said in a written statement. "Crews are on-site at two facilities to investigate protective relay conditions exacerbated by storm debris. We expect the final 32,000 affected customers in those areas to be restored within 7 to 10 days." The statement does not explain how debris affected the relays, nor does it describe what the crews found when they arrived.

Industry experts say the distinction matters. Protective relays are sensitive electronic devices that govern when circuit breakers open and close; relay logic failures can cascade through a substation and trigger widespread, difficult-to-diagnose outages. Utility consultant Barry Nguyen, who has advised on hurricane restorations in Louisiana and Florida, said CBPWA's language is notably guarded. "They're being careful about how they characterize this," he said. "That usually means they don't have a full picture yet, or that the picture they have is raising questions they're not prepared to answer publicly." State regulators at the Public Utility Commission of Texas and ERCOT have been notified, Odom confirmed.

The two substations serve portions of Corpus Christi's northwest residential corridor and the central business district, areas where some customers have been without power since Rafael made landfall fourteen days ago. CBPWA says it has rerouted load where possible through adjacent distribution feeders, but that full service restoration requires the facilities to be brought back online. The 7-to-10-day estimate is the first the authority has given for those customers. CBPWA did not indicate whether it has requested outside engineering assistance for the relay investigations, and declined to identify the facilities by name.

item.title: New boil-water notice for two Corpus Christi districts underlines utility strain
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The city says low pressure in part of the system means contamination cannot be ruled out. About 48,000 residents are covered, on top of a citywide notice already in force.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The City of Corpus Christi issued a boil-water notice Sunday evening for Districts 3 and 4, saying low water pressure in part of the distribution system meant contamination could not be ruled out.

About 48,000 residents are covered, the city said. The notice comes on top of a citywide boil-water notice that has been in effect since Sept. 18.

The city attributed the low pressure to storm damage to treatment and pumping infrastructure. The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost both power feeds during Hurricane Rafael and has been running on temporary pumps while the utility waits for replacement parts.

"Pressure in that part of the system is lower than we can accept," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokeswoman for the city water utility. "When pressure drops, we cannot rule out contamination. This is a precaution, and it is a necessary one. Boil your water. We are sorry to be asking again."

Gallegos said the notice would stay in place until pressure recovers and tests come back clean.

For the energy sector, the notice is another reading on how far the city's utilities are from normal two weeks after landfall. The ship channel remains closed by the Coast Guard, and crude exports have been halted since the day before the storm. But terminals, refineries and the workers who run them rely on the same water and power systems.

Market participants said the notice does not change the outlook for exports, which depends on the channel. One terminal manager, who asked not to be named because he was not authorized to speak for his company, said his site had its own contingency arrangements for water. "It is our people I worry about," he said. "They go home to this."

Power has not been fully restored in parts of the city.

The utility has not said when replacement pump parts will arrive.

item.title: Claims center opens for Corpus Christi spill as owners' liability takes shape
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The center, run for the tankers' owners, takes cleanup and property damage claims as federal oil spill law requires. Who ultimately pays may depend on an investigation that has barely begun.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — A claims center run for the owners of the two tankers involved in the Corpus Christi oil spill opened Sunday for cleanup and property damage claims, as federal oil spill law requires.

The center will take claims from people and businesses with oil on their property or cleanup costs from the spill. An estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived.

"The claims center is open," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "If you have oil on your property or you paid to clean it up, document it. Photographs, receipts, dates. Then file."

Under federal law, the owners of a vessel that discharges oil are responsible in the first instance for cleanup costs and damages, and must show they have the financial means to pay. Gulfwater Maritime Report reported that the tanker owners posted financial assurance with the Coast Guard.

For the tanker and insurance markets, the larger question is what happens afterward.

"The law says who pays first. The investigation decides who pays last," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics.

The Coast Guard has said investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems. If a third party caused the release, Holloway said, owners and their insurers would be expected to seek recovery. "That is years of lawyers. It doesn't change who writes the first checks," she said.

Claims so far are limited to cleanup and property. The state has closed Nueces and Corpus Christi bays to fishing and shellfish harvesting because of the oil, and commercial fishers have asked when claims for lost income will be taken. Whitaker said he had no date.

The ship channel remains closed. Crude exports from the port have been halted for two weeks.

item.title: Corpus Christi water plant on temporary pumps as utility waits for parts
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The O.N. Stevens plant lost both power feeds in the storm. The utility says damaged pumps need replacement parts and capacity is limited, a constraint for a city trying to restart its industry.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Corpus Christi's main water treatment plant is running on temporary pumps while the utility waits for replacement parts, limiting capacity ten days after Hurricane Rafael, the city water utility said Friday.

The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost both of its power feeds early in the storm and its pumps were damaged. Water pressure fell across the city, and a citywide boil-water notice has been in effect since last Saturday.

"The damaged pumps need replacement parts, and the temporary pumps can only do so much," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokeswoman for the city water utility. "We are sorry. We know how hard this is. Please keep conserving and keep boiling your water until we tell you otherwise."

Gallegos did not give a date for the parts or for lifting the notice.

The plant's status matters beyond households. Corpus Christi's ship channel is lined with crude terminals and refineries, and the city's recovery is tied to the same utilities its residents depend on.

"When people ask me what has to happen before this port is back, they expect a list of channel items," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Water is on the list. It is not a crude number, but it is on the list."

Holloway said she had no information that water supply was the limiting factor for any terminal. The ship channel remains closed by the Coast Guard while it is surveyed and the Inner Harbor oil spill is contained, and that closure is what is keeping exports at zero.

"Right now nothing can load because nothing can sail," she said. "I am watching utilities because they decide how fast things move once the channel opens."

The utility said crews are working at the plant around the clock.

The Coast Guard has not set a reopening date for the channel. Crude exports have been halted since the port closed to inbound ships ahead of the storm.

item.title: Eleven days without Corpus Christi: how the U.S. crude export system is bending
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Storage is filling, some buyers are looking at other Gulf ports, and ships are still waiting offshore. An analyst describes a system absorbing the gap rather than replacing it.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from Corpus Christi have been halted for 11 days. The port normally handles about half of the U.S. total. Sabal asked how the rest of the system is coping.

"The system is bending. It is not rerouting," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics, which tracks Gulf Coast crude flows. "There is no second Corpus Christi to send it to."

Holloway described three ways the gap is being absorbed.

Storage. Crude that would have loaded is sitting in tanks along the ship channel and at points inland. "That is the first cushion and the biggest. It is also the one with a hard limit," she said.

Other ports. Some buyers are asking about loading at other Gulf Coast terminals. Holloway said those outlets were busy before the storm and can take some extra cargoes, not all of them. "You can move a few ships. You cannot move a port," she said.

Waiting. Ships that rode out Hurricane Rafael at sea are back at the offshore anchorage. Their owners and charterers are paying to wait. "Every ship still sitting there is somebody betting the restart comes before it is cheaper to leave," she said.

What she is not seeing, she said, is producers cutting output because of the halt. "That is the step after tanks fill. I would not rule it out if this runs long."

Two developments this week added uncertainty without changing the physical picture, Holloway said. The Coast Guard said investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of the tankers involved in the Inner Harbor spill. And a vendor said its remote-access credentials had been misused.

"Neither one opens or closes the channel," she said. "But they tell you the investigation is not a formality, and investigations take time."

The Coast Guard has given no reopening date.

item.title: Tanker systems vendor says its remote-access credentials were misused; Corpus Christi exports stay halted
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Brightwake Marine Systems says it has revoked all remote access and is cooperating. Charterers are starting to ask which ships can be reached from shore.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — A company that maintains tanker cargo-control systems said Wednesday that its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused, two days after the Coast Guard said investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the two tankers involved in the Corpus Christi oil spill.

"Our remote-maintenance credentials were misused," said Owen Pryce, chief executive of Brightwake Marine Systems. "We have revoked all remote access to customer vessels and we are cooperating with investigators. We do not know who did this."

Pryce did not say which vessels were affected. The Coast Guard has not named any vendor in connection with its investigation and has released no findings.

An estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived. The ship channel has been closed since the day before landfall and crude exports from the port, about half of the U.S. total, remain halted.

For the tanker market, the disclosure raises a question that reaches beyond Corpus Christi.

"Charterers vet ships for age, inspection history and crew. This adds a line," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Who can touch the cargo system, and from where? A week ago nobody was asking. Today some are."

Holloway said she had no information on how many vessels use remote maintenance of the kind Brightwake provides. She said shore-based support for shipboard systems is common across the industry because it saves sending technicians to a ship.

She said the immediate market effect is limited because Corpus Christi is not loading in any case. "The channel is the constraint. This is about what happens after, and whether terminals and charterers want assurances before a ship comes alongside," she said.

Rendal Terminals has said it is cooperating fully with the Unified Command.

No reopening date has been set for the channel.

item.title: Corpus Christi crude exports stay halted as spill probe turns to cargo systems
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The ship channel has been shut since Sept. 13. An analyst says the Coast Guard's look at possible remote access to two tankers' cargo systems adds a new question for terminal operators.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from the Port of Corpus Christi remained halted Tuesday, eight days after the Coast Guard closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel to all traffic ahead of Hurricane Rafael.

The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports, analysts estimate, and its export terminals have been idle since Sept. 12, when the port closed to inbound ships with 14 vessels at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas. The Coast Guard has not announced a reopening date.

The outlook picked up a new variable Monday. Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, the two laden tankers whose release of about 9,000 barrels of crude at the Rendal Terminals berth was spread across the bays by the storm. Federal cyber teams are assisting.

"The market knows how to price a hurricane. It has a rough idea how long a Gulf channel stays shut after a storm," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "What it can't price yet is an open question about how two tankers' cargo systems behaved. Until that's answered, every terminal operator on the coast is going to look hard at who can reach its systems."

Holloway said the reopening timeline will depend on Coast Guard port conditions and the spill response in the Inner Harbor, and that buyers who rely on Corpus Christi barrels are watching closely.

"Corpus Christi isn't a side door for U.S. crude. It's the front door," she said. "Every day it's closed, someone has to wait or find barrels elsewhere."

The Coast Guard has said it will not characterize the cause of the spill until the investigation supports a conclusion.

item.title: Week ahead: four conditions for a Corpus Christi restart, and none is met yet
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: A surveyed channel, a contained spill, working utilities and staffed terminals. The first full week after Rafael begins with exports still at zero.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The first full week after Hurricane Rafael begins with crude exports from Corpus Christi still halted and no date for a restart. Analysts say four conditions have to be met first.

A surveyed channel. The Coast Guard has kept the ship channel closed while it is surveyed. Ships that rode out the storm at sea are waiting at the offshore anchorage.

A contained spill. An estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released from two tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth. Oil has spread into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. On Saturday the state closed both bays to fishing and shellfish harvesting because of the oil.

Working utilities. The city issued a boil-water notice for all of Corpus Christi on Saturday, and power outages remain widespread. Terminals need power for pumps, lighting and safety systems.

People. Dock workers, line handlers, pilots, tug crews and terminal operators live in the same flooded and powerless neighborhoods as everyone else. A federal major disaster declaration for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties was approved Saturday.

"Any one of those can hold up the other three," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The market is used to thinking about the channel. This time the channel is one item on a longer list."

Holloway said she was not attempting a restart forecast. "Anyone who gives you a date is guessing. What I can tell you is the order. Survey first, then the spill, because you cannot move ships through a response. Power and people run in parallel."

She said the fishing closure was a useful indicator for crude traders even though it has nothing to do with tankers. "It tells you the state thinks there is enough oil in that water to matter. The Coast Guard is looking at the same water," she said.

What to watch this week: any Coast Guard statement on the channel survey, the Unified Command's daily updates, and power restoration along the Inner Harbor.

item.title: Corpus Christi crude exports stay halted as spill response spreads across the bays
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The port has been shut for nearly a week. Oil in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays and a new fishing closure point to a slower restart, an analyst says.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from Corpus Christi remained halted Saturday, six days after the Coast Guard closed the port to inbound traffic ahead of Hurricane Rafael, as a spill response that began in the Inner Harbor stretched across Nueces and Corpus Christi bays.

The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports, according to analyst estimates, and loadings hit a monthly high in August. Fourteen vessels were holding at the offshore anchorage when the port closed to inbound ships; those that put to sea for the storm have since returned to wait for the channel to reopen.

The Unified Command estimates about 9,000 barrels spilled from the laden tankers MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth. Sheen covers about 33 square miles, and on Saturday Texas Parks and Wildlife closed fishing and the Texas Department of State Health Services closed shellfish harvesting in both bays. Navy salvage equipment has been requested. The cause is under investigation.

"Last week the question was how fast the channel could be surveyed. Now it's how responders want to manage traffic through oiled water," said Grace Holloway, an analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "That's a slower conversation, and buyers are already planning around it."

Holloway said cargoes normally lifted at Corpus Christi would have to be replaced from other Gulf Coast terminals for as long as the closure lasts, though those terminals cannot absorb all of the port's volume. She said traders would read the first Unified Command guidance on vessel movements closely for clues about timing.

"Nobody is going to rush tankers through a spill zone to save a few days," she said. "The market knows that. It just doesn't know how many days."

No reopening date has been announced.

item.title: Tankers return to Corpus Christi anchorage to wait as oil spreads across the bays
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Ships that rode out Rafael at sea are back offshore. The channel stays closed while it is surveyed and the spill is contained, and sheen now covers about 33 square miles.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Tankers that put to sea ahead of Hurricane Rafael have returned to the offshore anchorage at Corpus Christi, where they are waiting for a ship channel that remains closed with no reopening date.

The Coast Guard says the channel will stay shut while it is surveyed and the Inner Harbor oil spill is contained. Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi, has declined to give a timetable.

The spill has grown as a factor since the storm passed. Surge and wind carried oil out of the ship channel into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, the Unified Command said. Sheen covers about 33 square miles, with oil on North Beach and Portland shorelines and in marshes. Cleanup crews began deploying boom as winds dropped.

"The ships are back. The port isn't," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The market has stopped asking which day and started asking which week."

The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports, analysts say. Loadings have been halted since Sunday.

Holloway said the returning ships show that owners and charterers still expect to load at Corpus Christi and are not yet diverting in numbers. "Sitting at the anchorage is a bet that the wait is shorter than the alternative," she said. "That bet gets re-examined every morning."

She said crude that cannot load is accumulating in storage along the channel and at inland points that feed it. "Tanks are doing the work the ships would normally do. That works for a while," she said.

Two things would change the picture, she said: a Coast Guard statement on the channel survey, and a clearer account of how much oil is in the water near the docks.

Power outages across the area are also slowing the return of terminal staff and equipment checks.

No terminal has announced a restart date.

item.title: Petroleum hydrocarbons detected at city water intake; O.N. Stevens plant shifts to emergency filtration
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: TCEQ issued a water quality notice Thursday after total petroleum hydrocarbons were detected at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant raw water intake on the Nueces River, prompting an immediate switch to emergency filtration protocols.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality issued a water quality notice Thursday evening after petroleum hydrocarbon compounds were detected in raw water samples from the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant intake on the Nueces River, raising the first major environmental protection concern at the city's primary drinking water supply facility in the wake of Hurricane Rafael.

The O.N. Stevens plant, which treats surface water from Lake Corpus Christi and the Nueces River for delivery to roughly 500,000 people across Corpus Christi and surrounding service areas, immediately switched to its emergency filtration protocol upon detection of the hydrocarbons. TCEQ spokesperson Annette Vogt said the detection was identified during routine post-storm monitoring activated in coordination with the ongoing oil spill response in Corpus Christi Bay. "The hydrocarbon signature at the intake is consistent with petrochemical contamination that could be associated with storm-related runoff or the oil released in the Inner Harbor during the storm," Vogt said. "We are conducting expanded sampling to characterize the source and concentration."

City water utility spokesperson Teresa Gallegos said the emergency filtration protocol adds additional treatment steps beyond normal operations and that treated water leaving the plant currently meets all Safe Drinking Water Act standards. "We want to be very clear: treated water leaving the plant meets the standards for hydrocarbons," Gallegos said. "This detection does not change the conservation request already in place because of low pressure. We are activating additional treatment steps as a precaution while we determine the extent and source of the raw water contamination." She urged residents not to stockpile bottled water unnecessarily, noting that any change in treated water safety would be communicated immediately through the AlertNueces notification system.

Residents living near the plant in Calallen and in areas adjacent to the Nueces River were specifically notified by the utility as a precautionary measure given their proximity to the raw water intake area. TCEQ and the EPA Region 6 office are conducting joint sampling upstream and downstream of the intake to identify the contamination pathway. Bay monitoring data from the ongoing spill response is being cross-referenced to determine whether the detected hydrocarbons are connected to the Inner Harbor oil spill of Sept. 14.

item.title: Spill estimate of about 9,000 barrels at Rendal berth clouds Corpus Christi restart
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: A Unified Command names two tankers, MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay. For the crude market, the spill turns a storm closure into an open-ended one.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — An estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released from two tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth in Corpus Christi's Inner Harbor as Hurricane Rafael arrived, officials said Wednesday, complicating any timetable for restarting exports.

Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi and the Texas General Land Office have formed a Unified Command. It identified the ships as MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, the two laden tankers that stayed at the berth with Coast Guard approval when the channel closed Monday.

The cause is under investigation. On-water response is waiting for winds to drop, and Navy salvage equipment has been requested.

"Rendal Terminals is cooperating fully with the Unified Command," said Victor Lang, a company spokesman. He declined to discuss the cause.

The ship channel remains closed to all traffic. Crude exports through the port, which handles about half of the U.S. total, have been halted since Sunday.

"Yesterday this was a hurricane closure with a known shape," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Today it is a spill response, and those don't come with a schedule."

Holloway said the release itself is small against the volume the port normally loads. Its importance is where it happened. "It is inside the harbor, next to the docks, in the water the ships have to use," she said. "You can't run tankers through a cleanup."

She said buyers who had expected to reschedule cargoes for late this week were now being told there was no date to reschedule to.

Ships that left the offshore anchorage ahead of the storm remain at sea.

The Coast Guard has not said when the channel will be surveyed. Rafael made landfall near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. Tuesday as a Category 3 hurricane, flooding the bays with about 11 feet of surge and leaving widespread power outages.

item.title: Corpus Christi crude exports stay shut as Rafael lands; terminal spill adds uncertainty
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The top U.S. crude export port was already closed for the storm. A discharge at an Inner Harbor berth raises new questions about how soon loadings can restart.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from Corpus Christi remained halted Tuesday after Hurricane Rafael made landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm, and a reported oil discharge at an Inner Harbor terminal added a new unknown to the restart timeline.

The port accounts for about half of U.S. crude exports, according to analyst estimates. Loadings had been running at a near-record pace this summer and hit a monthly high in August. They stopped Sunday, when the Coast Guard closed the port to inbound traffic with 14 vessels at the offshore anchorage; those ships put to sea Monday as the channel closed to all traffic.

The Coast Guard said two laden tankers moored at the terminal were involved in the discharge. The volume and cause were not known Tuesday, and the agency did not identify the vessels or the terminal.

"The storm closure was a pause the market could plan around. A spill inside the harbor is a different animal," said Grace Holloway, an analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Until people know how much oil is in the water and where it goes, nobody can put a date on the first cargo out."

Holloway said buyers would watch three things in the coming days: the condition of the channel after roughly 11 feet of surge, damage to docks and tank farms, and any limits responders place on Inner Harbor traffic while they deal with the spill.

Power was out across much of the Coastal Bend on Tuesday, and damage at port facilities could not yet be assessed. The Coast Guard has not said when the channel could reopen.

"Corpus is the swing barrel for a lot of export books," Holloway said. "When it goes dark, everyone feels it."

item.title: Corpus Christi ship channel closed to all traffic; two laden tankers stay at Inner Harbor berth
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Condition Zulu is in effect ahead of Rafael's expected landfall near Port Aransas. Ships from the offshore anchorage have put to sea.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The Corpus Christi Ship Channel closed to all traffic Monday under Port Condition Zulu, completing the shutdown of the port that handles about half of U.S. crude exports.

Ships that had been waiting at the offshore anchorage have put to sea to ride out Hurricane Rafael. Two laden tankers remain moored at an Inner Harbor terminal with Coast Guard approval, said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. The Coast Guard did not name the ships or the terminal.

Rafael strengthened to a Category 3 hurricane as it neared the coast. Forecasters expect landfall near Port Aransas between about midnight and 2 a.m. Tuesday, with 9 to 12 feet of storm surge.

Crude exports halted Sunday when the port closed to inbound traffic.

"Zulu is the end of the part you can plan," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The rest is what the storm leaves."

Holloway said the market would look for three things after landfall: the condition of the channel, the condition of the docks and power, and how quickly the Coast Guard can survey the entrance. "A port can be undamaged and still closed, because nobody moves a loaded tanker through a channel that hasn't been checked," she said.

The two tankers left at the berth drew attention from traders, she said, because loaded ships normally leave ahead of a hurricane. Operators can ask to remain in port when sailing is not practical, and the Coast Guard decides case by case.

Terminals along the channel have shut down loading and secured equipment. Crude that was scheduled to load this week remains in tanks.

Holloway said storage would not be a constraint for several days. "The first week is about the weather. If there is a second week, that will be about something else," she said.

Sabal will report port status after the storm passes.

item.title: Corpus Christi crude exports halt as Coast Guard closes port to inbound ships
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Port Condition Yankee is in effect. Ocean-going ships are heading out, 14 inbound vessels are waiting at the offshore anchorage, and a hurricane warning is up for the Coastal Bend.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from the Port of Corpus Christi halted Sunday as the Coast Guard set Port Condition Yankee and closed the port to inbound traffic ahead of Hurricane Rafael.

Ocean-going ships are heading out to sea. Fourteen inbound vessels are waiting at the offshore anchorage, the Coast Guard said.

"Port Condition Yankee is in effect. The port is closed to inbound traffic and ocean-going vessels are departing," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi.

A hurricane warning was issued for the Coastal Bend Sunday afternoon. Forecasters expect Rafael to come ashore near Port Aransas as a Category 3 hurricane with 9 to 12 feet of storm surge.

Terminals began winding down crude loading Saturday, when the Coast Guard set the earlier Condition X-Ray.

"About half of U.S. crude exports just stopped moving," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The only number that matters now is how many days."

Holloway said a storm closure has two parts. The first is the storm itself, typically a few days. The second is the restart, which depends on what the storm does to the channel and the docks. "A clean pass and a quick survey is one outcome. Damage is another. Nobody can price that until it has happened," she said.

The 14 vessels at the anchorage will not wait there for the storm. Ships at anchor are expected to put to sea to ride it out if the Coast Guard tightens conditions further.

Crude that would have loaded this week will stay in storage along the channel. Holloway said tanks in the area have room for a short interruption. "A few days, the system absorbs. Past that, people upstream start making decisions," she said.

The next step would be Condition Zulu, which closes the channel to all traffic.

item.title: Corpus Christi crude loadings wind down as Coast Guard sets storm condition ahead of Rafael
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The port stays open under Port Condition X-Ray, but terminals are slowing loadings. Analysts say a closure would pause the gateway for about half of U.S. crude exports.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude terminals at the Port of Corpus Christi began winding down loading Saturday after the Coast Guard set Port Condition X-Ray ahead of Hurricane Rafael, warning that gale-force winds are possible within 48 hours. The port remains open, but ocean-going ships must plan to leave or get Coast Guard approval to stay.

The slowdown hits the largest U.S. crude export gateway, which handles about half of the country's crude exports and hit a monthly high in August, according to analysts.

"The first few days of a closure are a scheduling problem. After that, it's a market problem," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Everybody's question is whether the channel closes and how long it stays shut after the storm passes, and nobody can answer that until the surveys are done."

Holloway said cargoes scheduled to load at Corpus Christi in the coming days were effectively on hold. "Every cargo that was scheduled to load next week just moved to 'to be determined,'" she said.

Any ocean-going ship that wants to ride out the storm in port needs Coast Guard approval. The Coast Guard did not say Saturday whether any had asked to stay.

Holloway said buyers would look first to cargoes already at sea and to other Gulf Coast ports, but that no other single port could absorb the volume that normally moves through Corpus Christi. "You can shift some barrels around the edges," she said. "You can't move half the country's export trade to another dock on short notice."

Sabal Energy Wire will report on the anchorage, port status and market reaction through the storm.

item.title: Forecast cone now covers Corpus Christi; crude loadings continue, no port condition set
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Rafael's projected path shifted toward the Texas coast. The port is open, no watches are posted, and buyers are asking whether cargoes can load early.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The forecast cone for Hurricane Rafael shifted toward the Texas coast Thursday and now covers Corpus Christi. The port remained open and crude loadings continued.

No watches are in effect for the Texas coast, though officials are urging residents to prepare. The Coast Guard has not set a hurricane port condition.

"The port is open and our customers are loading," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "Any change in status will come from the Coast Guard Captain of the Port, and we will pass it on the moment we have it."

The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports, analysts say.

"Now it is a planning problem," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The crude that loads this week is safe. The crude that was going to load next week is a question."

Holloway said buyers with cargoes scheduled for the first half of next week were asking terminals whether loading could be brought forward. With tankers already waiting at the offshore anchorage and berths fully booked, she said, there is limited room to do so. "You can't pull a cargo forward into a slot that somebody else is using," she said.

If the Coast Guard sets a port condition, terminals would begin winding down loading and ocean-going ships would have to plan their departure. Ships at the anchorage would need to put to sea before conditions worsened.

Relief shipments are already being arranged along the coast, a sign of how seriously logistics firms are taking the forecast.

Holloway said the market reaction so far has been orderly. "People have seen storms before. What they have not seen is a storm aimed at this port at this volume," she said. "If it comes here, the size of the gap is new."

The next forecast updates will determine whether watches are issued.

item.title: Rafael becomes a hurricane in the southern Gulf; Corpus Christi loadings continue as market watches the track
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The storm crossed the Yucatan and forecasters warn it could strengthen. The port that handles about half of U.S. crude exports is open and loading.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Rafael became a hurricane Wednesday after crossing the Yucatan Peninsula into the southern Gulf of Mexico, and forecasters warned it could strengthen over warm water. Crude loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi continued without interruption.

Texas is among the possible targets in long-range forecasts. No watches or warnings are in effect for the Texas coast, and the Coast Guard has not set a hurricane port condition for Corpus Christi.

The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports, analysts say, and reported a monthly high for exports last week. Tankers continue to wait at the offshore anchorage.

"The market is watching one thing, which is whether the Coast Guard sets a port condition at Corpus Christi," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Until then it is a weather story. After that it is a supply story."

Holloway said the sequence, if it comes, is predictable. Terminals wind down loading first. Ocean-going ships are then told to leave or seek approval to stay. Inbound traffic stops, and finally the channel closes. "Exports go to zero a day or two before landfall and stay there until the channel has been checked," she said.

She cautioned against reading too much into the forecast this early. "The track can move a long way in five days. A storm that goes to Louisiana or Mexico is a different conversation," she said.

Shippers contacted by Sabal said they were reviewing loading dates for the coming week but had not changed them. One trader, who asked not to be named because of company policy, said buyers with cargoes due to load early next week were "asking the question, not giving the order."

Heavy rain ahead of the storm has already soaked the Coastal Bend this week, though it has not affected port operations.

Sabal will report any change in port condition.

item.title: Traders eye Tropical Storm Rafael's track toward Texas as Corpus Christi loadings run high
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Early forecasts show a west-northwest path. Analysts say the port's share of U.S. crude exports makes any Gulf disruption a market event.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude market participants turned their attention Saturday to Tropical Storm Rafael, which formed in the northwestern Caribbean with early forecasts showing it crossing the Yucatan Peninsula into the Gulf on a track that could reach Texas.

The timing is sensitive for the U.S. export trade. Crude exports from the Port of Corpus Christi hit a monthly high in August, and the port handles about half of U.S. crude exports, analysts said, leaving the market exposed to any disruption on the Coastal Bend. Tankers have been loading at a near-record pace and waiting at the offshore anchorage for berths.

"It's a long way from a tropical storm in the Caribbean to a closed channel," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "But with this much of the export market running through one port, people don't wait for the closure to start asking questions."

Holloway said traders and shipowners would watch for any change in Coast Guard port conditions at Corpus Christi, which would signal restrictions on vessel traffic. She said loading schedules for the coming week were the first thing likely to be revisited if the track held.

"Nobody reroutes a cargo on a Saturday forecast," she said. "They make a list of what they'd do, and they wait for Tuesday's."

She said the bigger question for the market was not whether loadings would pause, but for how long. A short closure ahead of a storm is routine for Gulf ports, she said. What traders price is the time it takes after a storm to inspect the channel, clear the anchorage queue and get berth schedules back to normal.

With the U.S. Labor Day holiday on Monday, Holloway said the first full read on market sentiment would likely come midweek. Sabal Energy Wire will track Rafael's path and any port status changes through the weekend.

item.title: Corpus Christi crude exports hit monthly high, cementing the port's outsized share
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Analysts say the Coastal Bend gateway now handles about half of U.S. crude exports, concentrating a large share of the trade in a single ship channel.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from the Port of Corpus Christi hit a monthly high in August, analysts said Tuesday, underscoring the port's outsized role in moving U.S. crude to overseas buyers.

The port now accounts for about half of U.S. crude exports, according to analysts who track Gulf Coast flows, extending a summer in which tankers were loaded at a near-record pace and routinely waited at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas for a berth.

"Half of the country's crude exports through one channel is a remarkable concentration," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "It's efficient right up until something interrupts it."

Holloway said the August figure reflected steady pipeline deliveries to the coast and a well-oiled routine at the terminals and the anchorage. "Nothing dramatic happened in August, and that's the story," she said. "The system just ran full."

The concentration also shapes how the market reads risk. Forecasters expect above-normal Atlantic hurricane activity for the rest of the season, and September is historically its peak. A storm that prompts the Coast Guard to restrict or close the Corpus Christi Ship Channel would pause loadings at the country's largest crude export gateway.

"September is the month this market watches the Gulf more than the price screen," Holloway said. "Nobody is predicting anything. But when one port carries this much of the load, the weather map becomes a trading tool."

Sabal Energy Wire will continue to track loadings and anchorage activity at Corpus Christi through the peak of the season.

item.title: Storm outlook puts a question to Corpus Christi crude buyers: what is the backup plan?
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Forecasters expect above-normal Atlantic activity for the rest of the season. Loadings are strong and the anchorage is busy, which leaves less room to clear ships before a storm.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Forecasters now expect above-normal Atlantic hurricane activity for the rest of the season, a seasonal outlook that crude buyers lifting from Corpus Christi are weighing against a loading schedule with little slack.

Loadings at the port remain near record and tankers continue to wait at the offshore anchorage. No storm threatens the Texas coast this week.

"The outlook doesn't change today's cargo," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "It changes how much you want riding on one outlet in September."

The mechanics are familiar to anyone who ships from the Gulf. When a storm approaches, the Coast Guard tightens port conditions in steps. Terminals wind down loading, ocean-going ships are told to leave or seek approval to stay, and the port eventually closes to traffic. Exports stop before the wind arrives and restart only after the channel has been checked.
