What is different this year is the starting point, Holloway said. "A port running this hard has more ships to move out of the way and more cargo backed up behind it when it reopens. The pause is the same. The line on either side of it is longer."

She said buyers have three practical levers. They can pull liftings forward when a threat appears. They can arrange alternative loading ports in their contracts. Or they can accept the delay and plan for it. "Most will do the third and call it the first," she said.

Sellers face the mirror image. Crude that cannot load has to sit in tanks, and storage along the channel is finite.

For now the market is treating the outlook as a reminder, not a signal. "Nobody trades a seasonal forecast," Holloway said. "They trade the cone, when there is one."

The peak of the season falls in the first half of September.

item.title: Corpus Christi crude loadings stay brisk as August winds down
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Export tankers continue to queue at the offshore anchorage as the Coastal Bend's crude gateway runs near a record pace, analysts say.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi stayed brisk through the third week of August, keeping export tankers queued at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas, analysts said.

The port has loaded crude tankers at a near-record pace this summer, reinforcing its position as the largest U.S. crude export gateway. Tankers calling at the Coastal Bend now routinely spend time at anchor before a berth opens.

"The pipes are full and the docks are busy," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "As long as Corpus keeps loading at this pace, the anchorage is where you see the strain, not the price."

Holloway said traders would watch two variables into September: freight availability for long-haul voyages, and the Atlantic hurricane season, which historically peaks in early to mid-September.

"A Gulf storm doesn't have to hit Corpus to slow it down," she said. "It only has to get close enough that the Coast Guard starts changing port conditions. Then the queue offshore gets longer, and everyone downstream starts making phone calls."

Holloway said buyers read the anchorage like a gauge. "Count the ships waiting and you know how hard the terminals are working," she said. "Right now the gauge says full."

For now, the anchorage is doing its job. Tankers arrive, wait their turn for a berth and a pilot, load and sail, and the next ship in line moves up. Holloway said the routine looked unremarkable from the outside, which was the point. "Nobody writes about a queue that keeps moving," she said.

Tanker-tracking firms will tally August loadings as the month winds down, and Sabal Energy Wire will report the totals when available.

item.title: Corpus Christi crude loadings stay strong into August; offshore waits persist
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Export terminals keep up a near-record pace as summer winds down; analysts see steady demand and a predictable loading rhythm.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude export loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi remained near record pace into mid-August, with tankers continuing to queue at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas for berth windows, market participants said.

The pace has held since early summer. Pipeline flows from the Permian Basin keep terminal tanks cycling, and charterers have kept tonnage positioned in the western Gulf to meet loading dates.

Terminal operators at Corpus Christi have added storage and dock capacity in recent years, and a deeper channel lets larger tankers load more crude per call. Freight market participants said the steady rhythm of loadings has helped charterers plan cargoes weeks ahead.

"Nothing about this summer has surprised us, which in this market is a compliment," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Barrels in, barrels out, ships waiting their turn. The machine is doing exactly what it was built to do."

Holloway said that predictability has its own value. "Buyers plan around Corpus because the dates hold, and they pay for that certainty in ways that never show up on an invoice," she said. "Reliability is a product too."

Late summer also brings a planned military movement through the port, as a Fort Hood aviation brigade ships its helicopters and equipment for an overseas rotation. Port officials have said military cargo will be handled alongside regular business, and the equipment is expected to move over general cargo berths rather than crude docks.

Sabal Energy Wire will continue weekly coverage of Gulf Coast export flows.

item.title: Explainer: one channel, two businesses — how Corpus Christi's refiners share the water with crude exporters
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The same ship channel that carries record export cargoes also serves the refineries along the Inner Harbor. Why that matters when the schedule is this full.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The export boom gets the headlines. The refineries were here first.

Corpus Christi's ship channel serves two energy businesses at once. Crude export terminals load tankers bound overseas, at a pace that is now near record. Refineries along the Inner Harbor take in feedstock and ship out gasoline, diesel and other products. Both depend on the same water.

"People talk about the export story and forget there is a refining town at the end of that channel," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics, which tracks Gulf Coast crude flows.

How the two fit together. Much of the crude that feeds both the export docks and the refineries arrives by pipeline from inland fields. The channel's main job for exporters is getting loaded tankers out. For refiners, the channel brings in some crude and feedstock by water and carries products out by tanker and barge, alongside pipelines and trucks.

Where they meet. Every deep-draft ship uses one entrance at Port Aransas and one route across the bay. A crude tanker outbound and a products tanker inbound are in the same lineup, handled by the same pilots and tugs.

Why it matters now. With crude loadings near record and tankers routinely waiting at the offshore anchorage, the lineup has little slack. A delay for one kind of ship becomes a delay for the other.

What a disruption would mean. Holloway said the two businesses would feel a channel interruption differently. "An exporter with no ships has no sales that week. A refiner has more options, because pipelines keep running both ways, but storage fills and product has to go somewhere," she said. "Neither likes it. They just dislike it on different timetables."

The port says the channel is open and customers' schedules are being met.

item.title: Army helicopter outload set for late summer at Corpus Christi; port says crude schedule holds
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: A Fort Hood aviation brigade will move its helicopters and equipment through the port for an overseas rotation. The cargo will share a channel already running near record crude volumes.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — A Fort Hood aviation brigade is scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the Port of Corpus Christi in late summer, adding a military outload to a ship channel that is already loading crude at a near-record pace.

The Army has described the movement as part of an overseas rotation. It has not given dates.

For the crude market, the question is berth and channel time. Tankers routinely wait at the offshore anchorage, and the daily vessel lineup has little slack.

"It goes on the same board as everything else," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "We have handled military cargo before. Our crude customers should not expect disruption. The docks involved are not the crude docks, and the transits are planned around the tanker schedule."

Maj. Darnell Price, a public affairs officer at Fort Hood, said planning with the port is under way. "The brigade's port movement is set for late summer," Price said. "Our soldiers will be ready when the port is ready."

Military sealift ships are large, and loading helicopters and vehicles takes days. The cargo does not compete for crude berths, but each sealift transit takes a slot in a channel where big ships largely move one at a time.

Market participants contacted by Sabal said they did not expect an effect on loadings. One shipbroker, who asked not to be named because he was not authorized to speak publicly, called it "a scheduling item, not a supply item."

The larger scheduling risk for late summer remains the weather. The outload is planned for the weeks when the Gulf hurricane season is at its most active, when any storm threat would reorder every movement in the port.

The port said it would publish no schedule for the military cargo.

item.title: Waiting time off Corpus Christi becomes a line item as crude loadings run near record
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: Tankers routinely queue at the offshore anchorage. An analyst says the wait is now part of the price of loading at the busiest U.S. export outlet.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude tankers continue to queue at the offshore anchorage as the Port of Corpus Christi loads at a near-record pace, and market participants say the wait has become a cost that buyers and shippers now budget for.

Tankers routinely wait offshore for a berth, the port and analysts say. The queue reflects demand for loading slots, not a restriction in the ship channel, which is open to all traffic.

"A queue is what success looks like at a port with one channel," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics, which tracks Gulf Coast crude flows. "Every ship out there is a cargo somebody wants. The wait has a cost, and at this pace the market has stopped treating it as a surprise."

Waiting time matters because a chartered tanker earns or costs money by the day. When a ship sits beyond the time allowed in its contract, the charterer typically pays the owner for the delay. Holloway said buyers lifting from Corpus Christi are increasingly writing the expected wait into their arithmetic before they bid for a cargo.

She said the pattern is likely to hold through the summer. "Nothing I see suggests the pace is slowing. If loadings stay here, the anchorage stays busy," she said.

Two factors could lengthen the line, she said. The first is any interruption at the berths, where little slack remains. The second is weather. The Gulf is entering the most active stretch of the Atlantic hurricane season, and a port that is running close to capacity has less room to clear ships ahead of a storm.

"That is a September conversation," Holloway said. "In July the story is simple. The crude is there, the buyers are there, and the ships are waiting their turn."

The port has said its customers' schedules are being met.

item.title: Corpus Christi crude loadings hold near-record pace as tankers queue offshore
item.dc:creator: Lucia Ferraro
item.description: The Texas export hub keeps its berths full through July; analysts say anchorage waits reflect steady demand rather than disruption.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi are running near record pace this summer, with export terminals working a full rotation of tankers and inbound vessels routinely waiting at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas before berthing.

The port's export docks draw crude by pipeline from the Permian Basin, and terminal operators have kept loading schedules tight through July. Anchorage waits have become a standing feature of the trade rather than a sign of trouble, market participants said.

"Corpus is where the Permian meets the water," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "When you see tankers lined up offshore, that's the market telling you the barrels are moving. The question traders ask isn't whether the docks are busy. It's whether anything slows them down."

Holloway said the steady pace gives buyers confidence in Gulf Coast supply, but that a hub running this efficiently has little room to absorb an interruption. "The flip side of being this efficient is that there isn't much slack," she said. "If something pauses loadings here, freight schedules feel it fast."

Market participants said Corpus Christi's role has grown alongside Permian production, with each new pipeline and dock expansion pulling more export volume to the Coastal Bend rather than to other Gulf ports.

For shipowners, the steady loading program has kept tankers positioned in the western Gulf, and charterers are watching berth availability closely as the summer wears on.

A port spokesperson has described the anchorage traffic as a normal part of a busy export season.

Sabal Energy Wire tracks Gulf Coast crude export flows weekly.
